## 2026-09-17 — B1c consolidated proxy response-lifetime repair

Root's initial Sol review found that the prior source removed a proof request
from the active set when its async handler returned, immediately after
`response.end`, rather than after the response's actual terminal event. It
also began `server.close()` before the promised teardown-503 interval and
could throw on drain timeout before bounded abort cleanup. This follow-on was
authored through native Sol HIGH. A separate fresh Grok review reached its
15-minute cap without an answer; that is no Grok verdict or approval.

The qualification-only proxy now holds each request until both the forwarding
handler and response are terminal. Successful `finish` completes the response;
premature close, request abort or either-side error on a proof-origin request
latches the fixed proof/request failure even after teardown begins. Only the
registered post-commit mint reply cut marks its own close intentional.
Controlled abort cancels each pending upstream fetch. The listener remains
open during the bounded proof drain so new background/poll requests are
classified as teardown and receive the fixed empty 503. Only after the proof
drains does close begin. Every preexisting-failure, drain-timeout and close-
timeout path runs bounded owned-server/socket/exchange abort cleanup before
engine cleanup; the first failure remains authoritative. `clientError` records
only a fixed category and destroys only the socket supplied by that server.

The private qualification config now requires nonempty `expectedSubject`,
adds it to the known-secret set and compares the actual trusted profile subject
to it. Root must independently obtain the existing synthetic user's stable
subject via a provider-side Keycloak admin read and put it in the private file
before an actual run. The harness neither performs that lookup nor derives the
expected subject from product output. The fixed issuer and independently
pinned subject feed the unchanged shared principal derivation. No provider
operation ran here.

Raw-authority observation labels now append only after all raw assertions and
clean owned-engine cleanup. The historical primary-positive/overall-negative
record and zero historical raw cases are unchanged.

## 2026-09-17 — B1d.2a managed organization policy source checkpoint

The identity recipe now has a separate `organizations.q` module over the
existing trusted OIDC profiles. It adds immutable-owner organizations,
admin/member memberships, pending/accepted/revoked invitations, expiring
one-per-organization/email reservations, append-only audit rows, live member
and reservation maintains, and a small nonsecret service-written policy.
Organization creation requires a fresh verified profile and atomically creates
the owner's admin membership and audit row. Capacity entitlement remains
service-only; there is no billing or plan integration claim.

`organizationRecordInvitation` is deliberately an owner/admin-authorized
digest-staging mutation, not server-random issuance proof. Acceptance hashes
the exact raw-token text with the forthcoming shared-interpreter `sha256`
primitive and performs pending, strict invitation-expiry, exact verified-email
and strict profile-freshness checks in the same transaction. A new member is
inserted tentatively before the live count enforces the current seat limit, so
a late capacity reduction rolls invitation, reservation, membership and audit
state back together. An existing member consumes a fresh pending invitation
without duplicating a seat or changing role. Owner identity stays immutable;
admins cannot remove admin peers, while the owner may remove a non-owner admin.

Recipient email matching is exact, case-sensitive UTF-8 equality; surrounding
whitespace is refused and no case/Unicode/dot/plus normalization, global email
uniqueness or identity linking is claimed. Invitation/reservation read rules
intentionally omit time inequalities. A stale but still verified exact profile
can therefore see bounded metadata, while preview and acceptance separately
require fresh proof. Audit rows and ordinary invitation projections expose no
token or digest. Hash-only table storage is not a claim about plaintext in a
later action result, step or delivery payload, and is not global erasure.

The focused sequential CLI test source sets profiles only through
`identityBegin`, `identityClaim` and `identityVerified`, then covers owner,
admin, member, recipient, outsider and other-tenant reads and writes; wrong raw
tokens and digest-as-token acceptance; revoked, consumed and expiry states;
false, missing, stale and exact-case profile evidence; exact proof and invite
boundaries; same-email distinct principals; reservation expiry/duplicates;
capacity denial and rollback; and role/removal/owner invariants. It requires an
explicit executable, expected SHA-256 and existing canonical owner-private
scratch parent, fails a digest mismatch before scratch creation, never defaults
to the published engine, and preserves unexpected output privately without
printing raw-token arguments. Source inspection of `verbs.rs` confirmed CLI
queries serialize under `data` and mutations under `result`; the test uses the
two shapes separately.

## 2026-09-17 — W12R1b: insert authority and the lead's three wrong records

The aggregate-copy detector now checks both unrestricted insert and update
rules and names the arms it proves unrestricted. In particular, restricting
update alone no longer silences an upsert whose first write uses unrestricted
insert authority. Its text says “through any mutation that writes it”, including
when the only current writer is a job; this is latent permission, not evidence
of an existing principal-callable score setter. Six equivalent unrestricted
rule spellings are exercised independently on both arms, with restricted,
private, immutable and unrelated-counter controls retained.

Three corrections are the lead's own errors. The lead removed the withdrawn
fresh-ranking claim from the card but left the README promising a recipe that
cannot compile against the now-expiring source. The README now carries the
card's actual aggregate-copy section, with a test comparing the complete
sections verbatim as well as the existing pinned card text. The lead's claim
that the replacement grep proved a stronger security property “by construction”
was false. The replacement binds every Quarry block in all 28 cards, three
published documents and both installable recipes, then checks both rules on
any table whose index includes an integer column. Its 49 blocks contain 99
such table occurrences and zero provably unrestricted write rules. It is this
indexed-integer invariant, not a proof about every possible ranking design;
the brief's leaderboard counterexample gains a score index in the regression.
The guard found the writes card's unrestricted ordinal insert, which now
requires the conversation's current ordinal. Its existing runtime journey
still sends 51 messages, retries them and pages their arrival order correctly.

The third error was the lead's assertion in §20.21 that sound indexed live
top-N requires sweeping every expired contribution first. Counts have a server
physical upper bound: stored count is at least live count. A descending
threshold scan could recompute candidates and terminate exactly once no
unseen bound beats the live heap, handling ties according to the promised
order and reporting incomplete on a meter cut. That read form is unbuilt,
not impossible. Signed sums do not have that bound, and live-valued device
snapshots do not preserve the server bound; such a read would refuse on
devices. The RFC, feeds and expiry cards, code explanation and binder diagnostic
now state that distinction. No index or new read form was implemented.

blocks with 408 bound table occurrences and zero aggregate-copy notes; the
installed feed and search recipes have 8 and 2 tables respectively and zero
notes. The retained-calibration survey remains explicitly ignored without
its external packets. No ceiling, serialization, existing corpus case or
publication changed. The lesson is that a prose pin must cover every published
copy, and a security assertion must inspect the bound schema rather than

- A rolling-24h ranking: `maintain trend: count likes by postHour, postAt, postId` with
  `by byScore: postHour, value, id`, read as a merge of 25 hour lanes with `where .postAt >
  now - 86400000`. 3,963 and 31,937 posts in the window: 265 and 276 examined, complete
  with `next`, p50 2.9 and 2.2 ms over loopback, top ten equal to an oracle, no
  out-of-window row. Zero-like posts are a second read of 25 examined. With `sync public`

## 2026-09-17 — ruling 32 measured, ruling 33 under blind review, ruling 30's design drafted (LLP 3000.007 §21.8, LLP 3000.007.001)

Work taken under the author's twelve-hour delegation; each decision is recorded as the
lead's in LLP 3000.007 §21.8 (L1–L6). Nothing is built and nothing is published.

- **Ruling 32's measurement** (`presence-cost/` in the derived-probes record; published
  0.2.27; a 50-member room; host load 30+, so shape not magnitude): 49 durable effect rows
  cost about 0.9 ms a send, about 18 µs a row. With 49 held polls a send's p50 rises from
  2.9 ms to 15–19 ms whether or not it emits — every commit wakes every held poll — and
  6,724 of about 7,800 connected-recipient decisions were already recorded as deferred
  effects, because under rapid sends most recipients are in grace between a poll's answer
  and its re-poll. Decision L4: build ruling 32 on the existing effect row, one per
  recipient. What a busy room pays for is the wake storm, which ruling 32 does not touch
  and which deserves its own look (a poll waits on the store's sequence, not on its
  partitions).

## 2026-09-17 — every commit wakes every held poll: measured and ticketed

Following ruling 32's measurement: the rise of a send's p50 with 49 held polls is not the
room's own fan-out. With 49 connected personas who belong to **nothing**, 160 commits into
one principal's private room produced 6,439 bystander `/changes` answers and doubled the
writer's p50 (2.07 → 4.00 ms, `dev --memory`, published 0.2.27); a bystander's answer names
the table the other principal wrote (`"tables":["messages"]`). The poll waits on the store's
one commit counter and `check` reports every table committed after `since`, unfiltered. LLP
3000.009 §7.1 already owns narrower observation and asks for this fan-out to be measured
first; the ticket (`issues/20260917-snapback4-every-commit-wakes-every-held-poll.md`) adds
that replica devices are woken too and that the wake is an activity side channel, and
suggests the smaller first step: wake a poll only for a commit that touched a partition its
principal holds or a table its watches read. Probes are in the derived-probes record.

## 2026-09-17 — two blind rounds returned: ruling 33 narrowed, maintained columns revised, a sync defect reproduced

Both commissioned reviews came back the same way: **GPT NOT READY, Grok READY WITH
CHANGES**, and in each the decisive High findings came from one family only. Records:
`llp/reviews/3000.007-ruling-33-expiring-mutation-pages.{gpt,grok}.md` and
`llp/reviews/3000.007.001-maintained-columns.{gpt,grok}.md`; dispositions in LLP 3000.007
§21.9 and LLP 3000.007.001 §10. Nothing is built.

- **Ruling 33.** The lead's argument — a query over the same prefix already shows the
  viewer its unswept population — fails when the mutation itself makes the prefix readable
  (a hidden gate row written, the page bound, the gate written back): abort versus commit
  then measures a prefix no query of that viewer can reach. And a predicting mutation can
  fail locally on a device-only unswept row and never reach a server that would have
  committed it. Revision 2 admits never-predicting mutations only, under a static
  stable-verdict condition, and is back with both families. The broader disclosure
  contract is left to the author.
- **Maintained columns (LLP 3000.007.001, revision 2).** The reservation the draft cited
  does not hide a parent's presence (it no-ops for a readable, unfiltered source):
  now unconditional and origin-keyed. Counting at a parent's birth leaked hidden
  population work: replaced by **limbo aggregates**, so birth and death are O(1). A column
  rebuild that reused `rebuild_maintain` would have **deleted every parent row**: the
  rebuild is in place, never deletes, and rewrites nonzero-to-zero on redefinition.
  Old images do not read 0 today: an implicit literal 0 and a named `Additive` exception.
  A 100,000-parent activation is one undeliverable commit: activation becomes a generation
  barrier with no row events. Rule probes from other tables could read the column: a
  resolved dependency walk, shared by binder and core. And the first build **does not
  predict the column on a device**, because of the next item.
- **A sync defect, found by the GPT review and reproduced on published 0.2.27**
  (`stream-image-ahead/` in the derived-probes record; ticket
  `issues/20260917-snapback4-stream-page-serves-images-newer-than-its-watermark.md`): a
  stream page re-materializes each `put` from the *current* row while its watermark stays
  at the log page, so a page ending before a device's own commit, and not acknowledging
  it, already carries its effect; the device replays the pending write on top. A public
  counter bumped by bob (seq 2) and alice (seq 3): alice's page from watermark 1 with
  limit 1 ends at watermark 2 with `n = 2`, and her pending `bump` replays to 3. Any
  predicted read-modify-write is affected; writes that set a value are not.

Learned, again: the design I thought was the careful one (ruling 33's "a query already
shows this") had the hole; and two families are not redundancy — of eleven High findings
on the RFC they shared one.

Implemented M0–M2 of LLP 3000.001's composition plan in the working tree for
lead integration, from base `70a663c22285dc3a5278ca9ac13db01bbe05446b`.
No commit, push, publication, ticket closure, or outside-sandbox qualification
is claimed. `Execution.components` is optional with serde default/empty
omission. The binder proves ownership over lowered IR; the device dispatcher
returns coverage for proven fields; the client requests the original query,
observes the device again, and publishes one composed ordinary `Read`.
The server and `contract.ts` are unchanged. The exact fixture is 25 retained
left rows and 26 authoritative held rows online, 25 and 25 offline, with
`complete: false`, `fresh: false`, no `since`, and no continuation online.
Transport failure uses the second whole local answer. Composed operations
delete any remembered server answer and do not cache their server reply.

The frame implementation mirrors coverage events; it never clears the
interpreter's global flags. Literal save/clear/merge would change execution:
scans and merges consult earlier cuts. The original global flags still
choose the first missing-fact text, whole-query completeness, cut, cursor,
dependencies, expiry and metering. There is one meter. An expression after
its cap is incomplete, including the returned expression of an earlier
binding. A shared guard after the cap withholds component coverage.

All paths retain the same global state and order:

  `:802` gates merge continuation; `:864` gates merge refill. These mid-run

Helper bodies are not opaque calls in IR. `bind/program/control.rs`
`helper_arguments` snapshots arguments once into fresh runtime names;
`fn_call` expands expression helpers in the caller, and block-bodied helpers
into fresh result/done bindings plus assignments/conditional statements.
The analysis sees all reads and top-level dependencies after expansion.
Fresh names prevent helper-local variables from hiding a caller binding;
nested writes may target only locals declared inside the inspected block.
A top-level block-bodied helper is conservatively ineligible because its
lowered top level is not bind-once. Expression helpers called from both
components pass. Inline multi-read aggregates are ineligible, as are their
bind-once equivalents; the final review added a red-before/green-after test
for this distinction. Multi-source forms that cannot prove independence
keep whole-query behavior.

## 2026-09-17 — MQ-R1: retained-read review fixes

Implemented the lead's dispositions against base `34a21aa90363728684e0bd64754cb84e04a82ed0`, after reading both `MQ-r1.sol.md` and `MQ-r1.grok.md`. Composition still requires both retained history and a component needing the server. Once entered, it keeps every second-local component for which the shared predicate does not want the server; completeness conjoins every locally kept frame with the server's word. The delayed third until-revoked component now stays deleted after an applied row deletion or scope tombstone.

Found point reads, including `exists`, mark only their component. `Reading::retained_group` also sets the old whole-query retention cell, so the new `Rows::retained_row` hook derives membership from the found row through `history::row_key`/`is_left` without that side effect. Misses retain the old unknown/null behavior. This deliberately follows the lead over Sol's proposed miss reclassification and over Grok's broader composition-entry predicate. Direct reading guards and escaped nested free names have no plan. The shared runtime frame still withholds an unclean forced plan. Meter charge refusals and read sites observing a cap mark their active frame; returning a previously completed binding does not inherit a later binding's cap. With examined=30, left keeps all 25 rows and its retained word; the later held read is capped. With examined=3, the subsequent reading binding is incomplete.

The new adoption qualification exposed a further defect: a program-only backend update cleared images and left-group metadata, and an old backend's delayed answer could publish. `device.rs` now preserves images for unchanged tables/maintains as well as the existing literal-default evolution case, and keeps their history metadata. The client advances its incarnation on successful adoption and drops remembered server answers. No durable or wire format changed. This small additional change in `device.rs` was necessary for disposition 8; the forbidden `web.rs`, `memory.rs`, serde plumbing, ceilings and `contract.ts` were not edited.

The actual-client file now has 21 scenarios per tier (42 total). New scenarios cover unique-index/id point hits, a miss and exists; complete-only composition entry's positive control; delayed current-row deletion and revocation; compatible adoption; store replacement; real guest-session rotation; prediction admission and settlement; expiry of one retained or held row using `POST /dev/clock/advance` by 7,200,000 ms and the device query's explicit clock input; interrupted replacement acquisition; and a same-store interrupted snapshot preserving retained history. Both delayed query and watch responses must actually reach the reply gate before the event runs. Every retained watch publication is checked for exact retained rows and incomplete coverage. Server-owned held fields preserve the one server transaction's observation; the next query observes held-row expiry. There is no claim of a common snapshot across the two hosts.

`witness/idb.mjs` now joins two dedicated rooms on the real server, leaves one, checks exact 25+26 online, 25+25 offline, reloads into a fresh realm with all network blocked, checks exact 25+25 from IndexedDB, and reconnects to exact 25+26. Composed observations are incomplete and not fresh. The command remains `node witness/idb.mjs`. Its extra Quarry was independently started through the existing `devServer` helper: `IndexedDB witness backend: 2 component fields; 0 compile errors`. The browser run itself cannot be claimed: Chromium exited with SIGABRT before the page existed. The lead must run that one command outside the sandbox.

## 2026-09-17 — retained-read composition: the lead's qualification, review record and landing

Lane MQ built the composition of LLP 3000.001 and two fix rounds took the
findings of three blind review rounds by Sol (gpt-5.6-sol) and Grok
(grok-4.6); the lane entries above carry their own commands. This entry is
what only the lead could run, and what the lead decided.

Outside the lanes' sandbox, on a machine whose load average ran between 15
and 75 all day. At `65bc84ac9`: `packages/snapback4/test/react.test.mjs`
13/13 and `retained-history.test.mjs` 42/42 on both tiers. The new
real-IndexedDB scenario in `witness/idb.mjs` then ran in Chromium for the
first time and composed correctly online (25 retained + 26 held), offline
(25 + 25) and after a fresh-realm reopen from IndexedDB (25 + 25); its one
failure was the scenario's own single-shot reconnect query, which raced the
client's in-flight offline retry. The lead first made that query poll for the
expected data (`d41c7dca1`); Sol's round-3 re-check rightly called that a
false-green risk, and it now waits, bounded, for `client.link()` and checks
the first online read. On the branch merged with `origin/main`
(`b58126b88` plus that witness change) the witness reports `composition:
{online [25,26], offline [25,25], reopened [25,25], reconnected [25,26],
fresh false, complete false}` and the React test is 13/13. The blocking suite
on that tree: builds, typechecks and fixtures green; client tests 587 of 596
with four timing failures in `transport-http` and the wide-snapshot
acquisition test; Rust green except
`clock_advance_preserves_a_live_action_claim_session_and_settlement`. Both
classes were checked against the exact base rather than called flaky by
eye: the clock test alone fails 2 runs of 3 at `70a663c22` on the same 5 ms
wall-clock tolerance (ticketed today), and the `maximum pending ids` transport
tests fail at `70a663c22` under the same load. An earlier full run at
`b5a7ddde3` is not evidence either way: most of its Rust test binaries were
killed with SIGKILL mid-run.

Decisions. The client keeps every field that would stay local as its own
query, not only retained ones, and still enters composition only when some
field is retained: an all-held query keeps its one fresh server answer. A
found point read of a left row marks its frame and nothing else; a miss is
unchanged. Fix round 1 also widened generation adoption so that a
program-only deploy would keep left history; one reviewer judged it sound and
the other showed it ignores `schema.auth`. It was reverted byte-for-byte
rather than patched, because it is a lifecycle this plan does not own, and it
has its own ticket. The mixed left/held ticket is closed. Left for the author:
whether `fresh: false` without `since` is the right card for a composed read.
No package version changed and nothing was published.

What the reviews were worth: across two full rounds the families agreed on
two findings of nine. Sol alone found the reading guard and the leaked nested
local; Grok alone found the over-broad cap note and the identity-mode hole in
the adoption change that Sol had passed. The lane also corrected its brief:
frames cannot save and clear the runner's flags, because scans read them
mid-run, so they mirror each event instead.

Round 2 on LLP 3000.007.001 (revision 2, limbo aggregates): GPT NOT READY, Grok READY WITH
CHANGES, both still "build this form"; records
`llp/reviews/3000.007.001-maintained-columns-2.{gpt,grok}.md`. Both families found the
same new channel — `/changes` reports touched tables unfiltered, so a source writer who
cannot read a parent learns from its own next poll whether the parent row was written. GPT
alone found that limbo splits one aggregate across two places whenever a parent is expired
but unswept (a valid sum refused, the sweep poisoned by an addition that no longer fits,
a redefinition with no owner for the stale half, a revived row with stranded debt), that a
"device load ignores supplied values" rule would zero a confirmed count on cold
restoration, that an insert's returned image is prepared before the engine writes (so a
maintained field in it is missing, fabricated or — if fixed naively — disclosed to a
creator who cannot read), and that generation discovery still depends on a row page being
deliverable. Grok alone found that a column maintain targeting the parent table would trip
`classify`'s maintain-target bypass and `refuse_engine_owned` for the whole application
table, that an implicit 0 stored as a literal default makes
`keeps_literal_default_images` true so devices keep rows reading 0, and that a sync
horizon ordered by the column makes delivery depend on it.

Revision 3 takes GPT's alternative rather than patching limbo: the declaration generates a
**private maintain** — today's machinery unchanged, the authoritative total for every
parent id — and the column is its **mirror** onto the live parent row. Birth is one lookup,
death does nothing, overflow has one home, a rebuild is today's `rebuild_maintain` on the
private table (where its delete loop is correct) followed by an in-place mirror pass. The
price is one small private row per nonzero parent, which all three Clique apps already pay
for the `maintain likeCounts` they declare. Also: the parent table is always named as
touched; write results never carry a maintained field; restoration preserves stored
values; the horizon joins the dependency walk; one reservation per attempt.

`issues/20260917-snapback4-oversized-sync-page-hides-generation.md` — an over-16-MiB
response is replaced by a bare `E_BOUND` body with no generation, the client only halves

## 2026-09-17 — W14b: the two-family implementation review, and what the lead changed

The lane's commit `0dac31c8aa` (base `ab061be930`) went to both families blind, read-only,
one brief of six questions: is every published block safe to copy; is every claim on the
card true of this engine; is the range-seek `remind` a complete replacement; do the tests
discriminate; does the one string change only text; coherence. Records:
`llp/reviews/3000.007-w14b-digest-card.{gpt,grok}.md`.

**GPT: READY WITH CHANGES — one Medium, wording.** The new digest paragraph said a schedule
"fires once per period boundary across restarts". `fire_schedules` (`engine/job.rs`) queues
only the *latest* boundary's period and then persists that boundary, so after three days
down a builder relying on that sentence would expect three digests and get one. The card
already said so eighty lines earlier ("Missed periods fire once, not once per skipped
boundary"); the new paragraph and the older general sentence both promised more. Applied in
all three places (jobs card ×2, README): a schedule never fires twice for the same
boundary across restarts; boundaries missed while the server was down coalesce into one run
for the latest period — and, in the digest paragraph, the consequence in the builder's
terms: a digest for a day the server was down is never queued. `tests/guide.rs` pins both
the new sentence and the absence of "exactly once".

**Grok: READY — three Low.** (1) Nothing pinned the job door in `why E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT`
(the card sentence, as opposed to the diagnostic's rewrite): pinned in `tests/guide.rs`.
(2) The example's `members` insert rule lets any member add any principal, who then
receives that chat's digest. That is a membership policy, not a job leak — `inbox` and
`digest` still walk only the recipient's own rows — but it is published Quarry, so the card
now says what the rule admits and points at the admin-gated form on the language card. The
reviewer's smaller alternative, `.principal = viewer or created …`, was **not** taken: a
bare `.principal = viewer` lets anyone join any chat and then read it, which is worse than
the policy it replaces. The rule itself stays, so the measured envelope (14,381 period
messages at 1,000 memberships) still describes the published schema. (3) No test had a
principal write `digestTotals`: `a_principal_cannot_write_the_job_written_totals` appends
one mutation to the published block and expects `E_RULE` with no row written.

The lead's first draft of that test was wrong in an instructive way: it expected
`Engine::mutate` to return `Err` for a rule refusal, and it returned `Ok` — a refusal is a
`WriteState::Failed { why }` inside the outcome, as the wire shows it. The test failed with
"a principal wrote the job-written totals table", which for one compile looked like the
deny rule not holding. It holds. The corrected test was then checked the other way: with
the block's `insert <- deny` swapped for `allow` it fails with the inserted row in the
message, so it discriminates.

w14b` 1 passed; `cargo test -p snapback4-sim --test clique digest::` 8 passed (the lane's

## 2026-09-17 — D1: instrument the web device and consolidate serde

Implemented only S0 and S1 of LLP 3000.002's proposed device representation and codec redesign, against base `70a663c22285dc3a5278ca9ac13db01bbe05446b`. These are dirty-tree measurements, not a publication or a browser-acquisition qualification. No ceilings, value forms, corpus cases, client contract, publication script, or S2 collections changed. The final measurement appends exactly one record to `metrics/wasm.jsonl` and sets the report-only gzip budget to 462,000 B. Missing or malformed budgets fail loudly; exceeding a valid budget only reports the overage and ticket.

`scripts/attribute-wasm.mjs` builds its own symbol-bearing web target, requires twiggy and the wasm target, prints the class table and generic census, and with `--families` enumerates surviving derived serde instantiations. It excludes debug/name sections, but includes 8,647 B of other custom metadata. The lead's reference attribution excluded all custom sections, despite describing only debug/name exclusion; it also classified some std generics over device types as device code. The table below replays the captured baseline through the final classifier so the comparison is like for like. Generic-item counts count distinct emitted functions, not distinct container type arguments.

The measured family is `Deserializer<StrRead>` and `Serializer<&mut Vec<u8>>`. `snapback4-core::json_codec` is the single funnel. Text preserves declaration order and all existing canonical bytes; typed values arriving through the dynamic dispatcher are consumed, rendered, dropped, and decoded, without cloning the argument tree. Merely doing that regressed apply: seven alternating blocks of seven runs measured 204.709 → 238.599 ms (+16.6%) for the 4,000-row page. The final implementation derives a small complete page-command envelope and decodes normal `apply`/`observe_store` calls directly from the original text. Refused or duplicate envelopes use the existing owned dispatcher. The envelope has no hand-written decoder and `StreamPage` still has exactly one definition. Both web and native hosts use this path. The final paired measurement below removes that regression.

Byte-identity audit, by site:

- `value::canonical_json` and `digest`, including `Schema::hash`, backend identity, and partition group keys, still serialize directly in the old declaration order. Host identities and stored identity comparisons therefore remain exact. The upgrade test reconstructs the old SHA-256 identities from direct `serde_json::to_string`, opens the kept store, queries its row, and checks that its first drain neither rewrites rows nor changes `memory:schema`. No reset or one-time re-projection is needed.
- `cursor::{encode_cursor,decode_cursor}` uses the text family behind byte adapters. Both v1 and v2 tokens have the exact old bytes and decode in both directions. Invalid UTF-8 still becomes the public cursor encoding error. `SnapshotCursor`'s decoder is also routed through the funnel; the server-only group decoders under the SQLite feature are absent from the web artifact and retain their existing text family.
- `memory::{row_key,parse_row_key,stored,parsed}` and `device::{encoded,decoded,open_store}` preserve the old row keys, tagged rows, staged rows, base images, outbox entries, backend texts, and metadata. Web `Change` envelopes use the same declaration order. The upgrade fixture explicitly constructs old `r/o/b/s/m` records and verifies they survive opening. `web.ts` reads outbox and metadata with `JSON.parse`, which does not depend on object key order; this change preserves the order anyway.
- `call::{parse,encoded}` preserves the typed value and the dynamic JSON result. A dynamic tree already has last-key-wins semantics; the owned argument funnel keeps those semantics and removes synthetic source positions from its errors. Original text entry points retain duplicate-field refusal and original positions. Direct page-command decoding falls back on duplicate fields, preserving the previous dispatcher behavior even for hand-crafted duplicate-key requests. The differential tests include duplicate top-level commands, page fields, and row fields.
- `engine::runner::charge_output` retains its original counting writer, moved into the funnel, and neither allocates a second result nor changes a counted byte. Consequently `Value` and its `ObjectFields` adapter legitimately retain two serializer families. The counter-specific surviving symbols occupy 3,211 shallow B across 18 symbols; this is attribution, not an isolated compressed-size delta. No IR or schema type retains that exception.
- `query_with_coverage` and `predict` now borrow their programs. IR clone glue remains because `Device::backend()` returns an owned backend: `Vec<Stmt>::clone` still occupies 6,395 B. All IR clone symbols move from 21 / 11,650 B to 20 / 11,652 B; removing the hot clones does not eliminate that cold getter's instantiations.

Shipped pipeline measurements (bytes):

| Artifact | Base raw | Final raw | Base gzip | Final gzip | Base brotli | Final brotli |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Device wasm | 1,891,742 | 1,573,696 | 520,557 | 461,566 | 394,881 | 358,696 |
| Generated JS glue | 11,325 | 11,325 | 3,047 | 3,047 | 2,700 | 2,700 |

The wasm gzip saving is 58,991 B (11.33%); the final size is 2,689 B above the scratch Value-family hack, while preserving byte identities, positions, ownership, and hot-path performance. The only product edit is the requested shared `PageArgument`: both owned and text dispatch deserialize the same `op`, `page` and `first` definition and execute the same page call. The missing-page diagnostic and non-boolean/missing `first` behavior remain the baseline's. A thread-local route marker exists only under `cfg(test)`; the tests live in `tests/codec/route.rs`, included in the unit-test build because integration tests cannot see a library's `cfg(test)` items. They assert direct pages and duplicate-field fallback on both memory and SQLite. The shared 188-scenario harness now sends `apply` and `observe_store` through `call_text`; other commands and the explicit owned-page differential retain `call()` coverage.

The codec differential compares every adapter with the actual pre-funnel API on the same input: text with `from_str`, owned trees with `from_value`, slices with `from_slice`, and each of `to_string`, `to_value`, `to_vec` independently. It covers 12 compilable reference/fixture backends and 307 loadable corpus programs, omitted/defaulted fields, renamed variants, custom text formats, duplicate struct and nested JSON keys, upper/lower hex, signed i53 edges, `9223372036854775808` and `18446744073709551615`, floating/exponent JSON values, depth 120/127/128/130, serialization errors, and non-UTF-8 slice refusals. For non-UTF-8 the existing funnel reports its UTF-8 conversion error rather than serde_json's positioned syntax error: refusal parity is asserted, not a false claim of identical error Display. The two owned-argument diagnostics additionally pin the literal baseline Display and its text-parser position suffix. Page dispatch is checked against an independent baseline oracle using plain `serde_json::from_value::<StreamPage>` on the subtree, not against the new owned path alone.

The durable fixture is nine literal `{s,k,v}` texts produced once with plain `serde_json` calls mirroring 0.2.27's baseline encoders; the exact recipe is in `tests/codec/old_store.rs`. It includes the schema and backend hashes, stored backend, acquired/generation metadata, a row and row key, outbox, base image and staged row. Open/read keeps all records. First drain consists exactly of the baseline's re-emission of `device:backend`, `device:backend-identity`, and `device:generation`; it rewrites no row, outbox, base or staged record and does not reset. The reverse check decodes newly written envelopes and each record with plain serde and checks frozen bytes/values, including production's queued and staged writers. SQLite opens and queries values persisted through the pre-funnel serde APIs and retains the base/staged images. These are compatibility guards that should also pass the baseline, not proof that S1 is wired.

The blocking suite's existing client-test glob now includes `wasm-codec-census.test.mjs`. It reads all device sources except the three native-only files and the five named core paths, names file and line on direct typed serde entry points, and keeps exact-line exceptions with reasons for SQLite-only partition code. Test or dynamic-envelope exceptions require the same explicit data; no entire module is silently exempted. The source census itself took 2.765959 ms in `node --test packages/snapback4/test/wasm-{codec-census,budget,families}.test.mjs`. The synthetic mutations cover central parse/encode, MQ components and `Vec<String>`; actual production substitutions in `call.rs` were also made and restored, individually, and the real census test killed all three.

The route probe now increments inside `page_call` and the owned fallback and counts the call site's actual `json_codec::from_value` invocations under `cfg(test)`. A direct page has one page call, no fallback and zero owned conversions; a duplicate-field page has one page call, one fallback and one owned conversion. The owned dispatcher can reach the same page routine, so observing the page routine alone is insufficient: the conversion counter is what kills the reviewer's parse-to-tree mutant. There is no production probe or extra traversal.

Native owned-tree adapters now deserialize their rendered text with recursion limiting disabled. Ordinary `from_text` remains bounded. A 160-array programmatically constructed `Json` is compared through both owned adapters to the plain serde APIs; it cannot be manufactured first by the ordinary text parser. `serde_json/unbounded_depth` is enabled only on non-wasm32 targets, with no `Cargo.lock` change. The web trial of this feature grew the module by 7,417 raw bytes and 436 gzip bytes, so it was not retained on the web, whose host inputs are text.

The artifact checker now checks allowed families across all typed entries, including standard containers and types that occur only with an owned reader. It resolves `Vec<_>` visitor symbols to their concrete element type, treats the map-key serializer as its underlying writer, and distinguishes derive refusal/formatting helpers from input readers. The unchanged artifact disproved one literal premise of the brief: the dynamic JSON envelopes necessarily contain `Value`/`Number` Display writers and `json!` scalar serializers for `String`/`&str`, in addition to the typed family and counting writer. Those exact type/family pairs are explicit exceptions; no typed container or owned decoder is excused by them. Unknown concrete families still refuse. The exact Value/ObjectFields counting-writer exception is retained, including Value's own derive helper. Surviving symbols cannot prove anything about a fully inlined instantiation; the production source census supplies the independent wiring check. `measure-wasm.sh` runs `--check-families` before measuring and refuses before appending a record if it fails. Its dirty pathspec now includes the compiler pin and budget; stubs exercise each and prove family failure cannot emit a metric.

The literal 0.2.27 store fixture is compatibility evidence, not S1 wiring evidence; it is a frozen recipe of the baseline encoders, not a captured IndexedDB dump. SQLite now snapshots every raw row of `r`, `_device_outbox`, `_device_base`, `_device_snapshot` and `_meta` before and after open and compares exact SQL values (including exact text bytes). A transient production-open mutation appending whitespace only to row and outbox JSON remained semantically readable but failed the new raw equality. return `(Value, key)`; SQLite and Postgres join and decode the row, and both
memory stores clone it. A real key-only head needs a new bounded index-head
method on `Rows`, implementations in SQLite, Postgres, core MemoryRows and the
device MemoryTx, forwarding through Reading/Predicting, then deferred row
materialization in the heap. Estimate: seven production files, roughly
200–350 lines plus store/engine/device tests. Expiry, filters, further terms
and live aggregates that require source rows need the existing materializing
path. No prototype or head-only speedup is claimed; that extension is for the
lead's decision.

## 2026-09-17 — maintained columns: two gates measured by proxy; the horizon gate fails and finds a P1

LLP 3000.007.001 read READY from both families this morning; its §7 asks for three
measurements before a lane is briefed. Nothing is built, so the lead measured with the form
the column replaces — a hand-kept count column whose `update` puts the parent row on every
like — which is byte-for-byte what §3.5's mirror would put. Published `snapback4@0.2.27`
binary; record `benchmarks/runs/2026-09-17-snapback4-derived-probes/column-gates/` and
`horizon-gap/`.

**Gate 1** (100,000 likes over 2,000 posts, a bystander device following the log; on-disk
store, checkpointed, against a zero-like baseline). Per like — wire / log / database
growth, bytes: column 823 / 851 / 1,794 on a 500-byte parent and 4,323 / 4,351 / 5,667 on a
4,000-byte one; synced maintain 329 / 334 / 1,170; `online only` 182 / 190 / 997. The like
row is 182 bytes in every form, so the count's own cost is 641 B as a column against 147 B
as a maintain row (4.4×), 4,141 B on the large parent (28×). The gate's letter ("no worse
than the hand-kept score") is an equality the lane asserts; what the numbers change is how
loud `N_MAINTAINED_COLUMN_STREAM` has to be.

**Gate 2** (the workload pinned before measuring: the Clique scale fixture's recorded like
stream, unmodified; a device acquiring `last 2000 by byTime` at the 50% checkpoint). The
engine sent the device **1,165 distinct posts beyond its horizon** in the replay's
remaining 7.7 hours — **58.3% against a 10% threshold**; an analysis of the fixture alone
gives the same 1,165. By §3.6's rule, written before the measurement, a device-side repair
is designed and reviewed before the first build ships on a horizoned table.

**Then the real finding.** Asking what a device does with those rows: its coverage rule
(`engine/read.rs`, after the scan loop — same index, descending, more rows held below)
assumes the rows it holds on the horizon index are a contiguous newest suffix. They are
not, once any old row has been updated. On the **published client** (wasm device in Node),
`sync public last 5 by byTime`, twelve posts, `posts after c last 3 by byTime`: before any
like the pages are `p12 p11 p10`, `p09 p08 p07`, `p06 p05 p04` (the page crossing the
horizon goes to the server). After alice likes `p02` and `p04`: `p12 p11 p10`,
`p09 p08 p04`, `p03 p02 p01` — **three posts skipped, every page `complete: true, fresh:
true`.** Filed P1: `issues/20260917-snapback4-device-page-past-horizon-answers-from-
scattered-rows.md`. It predates this program: the hand-kept `score` three Clique builders
wrote causes it, and so does an edit to an old post. No fixture or calibration could have
seen it, because each starts from a fresh device and a fresh snapshot repairs it.

Decision L14 (LLP 3000.007 §21.8, the lead's, under the author's delegation): the horizon
repair precedes maintained columns; gate 5 (activation) cannot be measured before the
mechanism exists and becomes the build lane's milestone zero, with a stop. The repair's
direction is in the ticket — a device knows a horizoned group exactly at and after the
boundary key it acquired and nothing below it; `apply` declines an unheld row below that
key — and it is handed to the wave 13 lead, who owns read completeness.

Learned: a threshold stated before a measurement earned its keep twice — it failed
honestly, and chasing *why the number mattered* found a wrong-answer defect that a growth
metric alone would have filed under memory. Second: "measure by proxy" was legitimate here
only because the proxy is the same log event, not a similar one; the record says so at the
top of each table. Third: the first draft of the gate-1 probe measured the WAL, not the
store (10 KB a like); checkpoint a copy and subtract a zero-like baseline.

```text
E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT: loop over members[roomId] first 20 by byRoomPrincipal: members by byRoomPrincipal (page bound 20): the literal page bound must cover the schema cap 100
```


N_NO_CURSOR cap clause (Q3):

Before:

```text
N_NO_CURSOR: query probe returns a page of 50000 inbox rows with no cursor: when more rows exist the card reads `complete: false` and there is no `next` to continue on
rewrite: declare `c: cursor ?` and page with `after c` — probe(.., c: cursor ?): return inbox[..] after c last 50000 by <index>; a table `cap N by column` can replace a cursor for a single plain group page that pins column and covers N within the examined ceiling; this page still needs continuation
```

After:

```text
N_NO_CURSOR: query probe returns a page of 50000 inbox rows with no cursor: when more rows exist the card reads `complete: false` and there is no `next` to continue on
rewrite: declare `c: cursor ?` and page with `after c` — probe(.., c: cursor ?): return inbox[..] after c last 50000 by <index>; read the whole group: `t[..]`, when its schema cap fits the examined ceiling; otherwise this page still needs continuation
```

## 2026-09-17 — W13g stops at the acquisition-wire condition; the horizon regressions are red

Base: `a1afab4e3625a64ffb80d19bf6cd83fc1f3a0b38`. No product implementation,
wire change, ceiling change, commit or publication. The lane's explicit stop
condition applies: “Do not change the wire form of a snapshot or the stream
unless the boundary cannot be recorded without it; if it cannot, stop and say
so.” The added `crates/snapback4-device/tests/w13g_probe.rs` retains the two
requested red regressions and executable evidence for that stop. Its red
tests are intentional unfinished acceptance, not a green landing candidate.

**Design and the obstruction.** The coverage rule must distinguish an acquired
suffix from arbitrary holdings, as LLP 3000.007 §20.22 requires. The proposed
mutable-key policy is to keep an already held row when its key moves below the
boundary: point reads and delivered history still own that row, while a
descending suffix page excludes it. A put moving an unheld row above the
boundary becomes part of the known suffix. This choice is unimplemented;
the move-below/move-above acceptance tests remain owed. A continuous live
renewal keeps the old boundary; acquisition after a gap replaces it, even
when older rows remain held. That renewal acceptance remains owed too.

The missing input is an authoritative acquisition boundary. `expand_joins`
in `partition.rs` chooses the newest N candidates from `group_at(join_seq)`,
then `stream` replaces each candidate with its current row image. A mutable
ordering key can therefore disappear before the device ever sees it. A
device cannot safely treat the oldest delivered image as the acquisition
floor. The following two histories, tested with `retain delivered-history`
so that `joined` is present, produce identical snapshot and stream payloads,
including event sequence numbers:

| History | Before joining, `p1.at`, `p2.at`, `p3.at` | `last 2` acquisition floor | After joining |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1000, 2000, 3000 | `p2` at 2000 | move `p2.at` to 500 |
| B | 700, 800, 3000 | `p2` at 800 | move `p2.at` to 500 |

Both streams contain `p3(at=3000, seq=2)`, `p2(at=500, seq=2)`,
`p2(at=500, seq=3)`, `joined: {posts: [["g"]]}`, watermark 3, generation 1,
and `more: false`. Neither contains `p1`, although each server's current
descending page is `p3 p1`. Inferring the floor at 500 would promise a known
suffix containing a row the device never acquired. The boundary values
2000 and 800 are absent from both payloads. Reading `seq`, which the current
device event struct discards, cannot recover them. The test asserts equality
of both complete modeled payload histories and pins the server positive.
Backend store identity is independent random incarnation metadata, not an
encoding of a boundary; no inference can come from that field either.

There is a separate empty-group ambiguity. With an online-only membership
table and default until-revoked retention, a snapshot for an acquired empty
group and a snapshot for a never-acquired group are byte-identical after the
ordinary JSON serialization: empty events, `held: {}`, watermark 1 and the
same generation. Snapshot `held` and stream `joined` currently enumerate
delivered-history tables only. Thus the requested `whole` versus no-boundary
distinction also lacks an input. Extending the audience lists alone would
address that ambiguity but would not restore the lost ordering key above.

The lead needs to authorize a protocol carrying a group acquisition's
table/index/prefix and encoded floor or `whole`, with an ordering relative to
puts and scope tombstones and publication only after staged acquisition and
catch-up. Snapshot group completion, first acquisition, continuous renewal
and re-acquisition must be distinguished; ordinary puts must never widen
coverage. This is a proposed next design step, not an implemented or reviewed
wire format. Selecting a guessed floor, counting all puts in a stream page,
or dropping every old put cannot satisfy the accepted brief. The related
current-image/watermark ticket is therefore relevant to this lane, not merely
an independent growth concern.

**Measured before the fix.** On SQLite and memory, cold page 1 is
`p12(0) p11(0) p10(0)`, complete, with next and no unknown; cold page 2 is
`p09(0) p08(0)`, `complete: false`, `cut: null`, no next, `unknown: true`.
After streamed likes of `p02` and `p04`, page 1 is unchanged and page 2 is
`p09(0) p08(0) p04(1)`, `complete: true`, `cut: null`, with next,
`unknown: false`. Both stores gain exactly **2** unheld old rows. The pinned
server page is `p09 p08 p07`. These are the two red regressions; no after-fix
result exists because no fix was authorized past the wire stop.

The original `horizon-gap/measure.mjs` also ran against this worktree's built
binary and built wasm/client package, not an npm publication. Its verbatim
output is `/private/tmp/w13g-client-probe.log`. Before likes, its client pages
are `p12 p11 p10`, `p09 p08 p07`, `p06 p05 p04`; after likes they are
`p12 p11 p10`, `p09 p08 p04`, `p03 p02 p01`, every page
`{"complete":true,"cut":null,"fresh":true}`. Server pages remain
`p12 p11 p10`, `p09 p08 p07`, `p06 p05 p04`. The raw device and client
observations reproduce the ticket on the exact base above.

**Scope left open.** Boundary recording/persistence/reset, the suffix read
rule, put filtering, whole-group completeness, reopening, activation,
renewal, both mutable-key directions, hidden-world coverage comparisons and
the wasm regression's green result are not built. The README, sync card,
NOT-DOING, diagnostic catalogue and existing source are unchanged. No new
diagnostic or diagnostic-text change exists. The raw boundary-key count at
1,000 groups of `last 500` is **1,000**, independent of the 500,000 acquired
rows. Persisted metadata framing and storage overhead are unmeasured because
there is no implementation. Verification and raw encoding measurements follow
below in this same entry.

The encoding test uses the chat table's real `byConvTime` index and 32-byte

keys**. This is an encoding measurement for that ID shape, not a persisted

## 2026-09-17 — W13c-2: range/list merge lanes and time index keys (rulings 28–29)

Continued from W13C at `4a1bbf4495e4ccff4e2744cc73c42e3b1c01df43`, preserving
its prefix reads, cap-derived bounds, prefix existence and P2 setup hoisting.
A query lane now takes the statement loop's domains except walk: a prefix
page, an integer range, or a bounded list argument/expression. `LaneSource`
is `Scan | Range | List`; range/list binding and evaluation reuse statement
loops. Bounds evaluate once, lists retain their order, duplicate lanes still
deduplicate rows, and empty domains are complete. Literal or common-expression
widths and list bounds supply static counts; other widths print `lanes ≤ meter`
and do not emit N_WIDE_MERGE. Jobs retain literal/table merge lanes inside
chunks; the new domains are query-only. Mutation pages remain unchanged.

The range itself is not materialized. Uniform merges retain lane descriptors
under an upfront heap charge (including vector spare capacity, owned prefix
keys and cursor/seek bounds), then use the existing head strategy. Non-uniform
traversal is unchanged. A billion-lane empty range stops at the unchanged heap
ceiling in under 100,000 steps; it cannot allocate a billion descriptors.

Table `by` and `unique` lists now take `day`, `hour` and `bucket` of a required
local time column, at any position, once per function per index. The compiler
uses maintain argument validation and the stores share CalendarKey's evaluator
with maintain groups. Integer key names support positional pins, function-name
seeks and cursors, without adding row fields, writable values, rule fields,
cap keys or sync audience keys. Computed indexes are not plain. Job cursors
check immutability of the underlying time column. Updates and adoption rebuild
through the ordinary index paths, including changes of period/offset. A real
column colliding with a function name is refused with a rename rewrite.
Malformed computed expressions and empty calls produce diagnostics, not panics.

Published examples are a room/hour listing and a daily unique check-in; the
language card compiles and runs them. The indexes, reads, language, maintains
and code-explanation cards and package README move together. No new card word
or diagnostic code was added, no ceiling or Value serialization was changed,
and no existing conformance case was edited. The two ruling implementations
are annotated once each with LLP 3000.007 §21.6.

Measured on one 1,200-post, 25-lane maintained-count fixture, typed and range
ranking both examine **35** rows on the server and each device store, return
the same rows and cursor, and match the oracle. The base supports maintained
`value, id` suffixes, so ties use the maintained id; the oracle uses that exact
order rather than claiming a post-time tie order this base does not provide.
A **5,000-lane / 20,000-post** range on all three native hosts returns **10**
rows, `complete: false`, `cut: meter`, no `next`, **9,096 examined**,
**0 index entries**, **19,112 steps**, and **3,363,950 charged heap bytes**.
The examined count includes failed charges while the existing head-opening
loop visits the remaining lanes after the cut; the ceiling stays **8,192**.
A supplemental WASM/MemoryRows probe matched those rows/counts, with
**1,763,950 heap bytes** on wasm32. Its four scenarios passed; it was a scratch
harness, not a replacement for the native server/device suites.

The paired tests compare serialized pages, completeness, cut, cursor and every
meter field for worlds differing in hidden row contents, and for hidden/absent
worlds after acquisition on both device stores. There is a brief conflict for
server hidden/absent worlds: the unchanged non-uniform traversal's operator
meter counts physical rows. The same **50 visible** rows with **0 versus 50
hidden** rows produce byte-identical page/complete/cut/next but **50 versus
100 examined**. An isolated harness over the exact base core/lang sources
reproduced those numbers. The test records the limitation instead of changing
or disguising the existing traversal. No claim of hidden/absent equality of
the server's raw operator meter is made.

Other differences from the adopted brief: this base's lane refusal says
“prefix read”, not the published 0.2.27 “bounded range read”; Wave 12's
25-literal-lane Trending example is absent, so the conditional feeds rewrite
was not performed and existing feed prose was not reformatted. The checked-in
§21.8 does not contain L5, but the lead's explicit any-position ruling in the
brief was implemented. Ruling 30's count-on-row design remains unbuilt, as asked.

## 2026-09-17 — W13g-2 carries the acquisition boundary and pages by it

Base: `a1afab4e3625a64ffb80d19bf6cd83fc1f3a0b38`. This continues the preceding
entry after the author's explicit authorization of an additive acquisition
wire field. No commit, push, publication, ceiling change, value serialization
change, eviction or backfill. The predecessor's entry is unchanged.

**Design.** Snapshot and stream replies add optional `acquisitions`:

```json
{"acquisitions":[
  {"at":0,"table":"posts","index":"byTime","group":["g"]},
  {"at":2,"table":"posts","index":"byTime","group":["g"],"floor":"056700000480000000000007d006703200000670320000"}
]}
```

Each marker applies before `events[at]`; `at == events.length` means after
all events. A missing `floor` begins acquisition; a completion supplies
`"whole"` or the hex encoding of the full `rows::index_key`, including its
appended row ID. A begin and completion can share a position for an empty
group. This is a separate field, not a new event kind: older clients ignore
unknown reply fields, and events, sequence numbers, `held`, `joined` and
watermarks keep their forms and meanings. The TypeScript client does see and
forward it to the device, so `local.ts` now types `AcquisitionMarker` and the
optional field on its transport page; the public Read/Write card is unchanged.
Native and wasm deserialize the same Rust `StreamPage`.

`partition.rs::snapshot_page` records the scan's selected key as `at.after`
and publishes a completion only when `group_rows_from` finishes that group;
it re-encodes the group and that stored-key suffix, not a subsequently updated
row. `expand_joins` selects from `group_at(group_partition, event.seq)`, sorts
by the horizon's encoded index key and truncates to N. Immediately after that
selection it captures the oldest selected key (or `whole` for fewer than N).
Only later does `stream` replace candidate images with current readable
images. Its marker offsets are remapped when current visibility suppresses
an event, preserving ordering before subsequent puts or scope tombstones.
A continuous live renewal emits no markers; a replacement after expiry emits
the scope first, then the new acquisition. Current authorization also gates
boundary publication; metadata is not a way to retrieve a revoked group.

`device/boundary.rs` owns the persisted map at
`device:acquisition-boundaries`, keyed by JSON `(table, index, hex group
prefix)`. A null entry denotes an unfinished acquisition. Snapshot markers
and catch-up use `device:snapshot:boundaries`; the existing snapshot owner,
generation, send-revision and watermark guards fence that state, and publication
copies it alongside the staged rows in one transaction. Replacement retains
boundaries only for retained left groups. Reacquisition replaces the boundary;
clear/reset and a schema change requiring acquisition clear it. A completion
for a group without a matching begin, or with an invalid index/prefix/key, is
ignored and reported both to stderr and in `device:acquisition-report`:

```text
ignored acquisition boundary for posts.byTime: group is not acquiring or boundary is invalid
```

Ordinary puts neither create nor move a boundary. An unheld put below it is
dropped, including during staged catch-up; held puts and deletes still apply.
A held row whose key moves below it stays held for point reads, but descending
suffix pages stop before it. A put moving above it joins the suffix. The
interpreter obtains the boundary through `Rows::acquired_boundary` on the
reading and prediction adapters. A full page stops at its last returned key;
an exhausted shorter page must also prove that its range ends within the
boundary. Otherwise it reports incomplete/unknown and the client falls back.
`whole` proves the group's end, including acquired empty groups. Missing
metadata stays unknown. Other indexes, ascending reads, existence scans and
the merge algorithms are unchanged. Excluding a straggler requires a guard
inside the existing scan loop as well as replacing its final coverage test;
the original brief's suggestion that only the after-loop check would change
was insufficient for its mutable-key requirement.

**Measurements and regressions.** On both SQLite and persisted memory,
1,000 group boundaries for the `last 500` envelope occupy **114,000 raw key
bytes**, **228,000 hex floor bytes**, **338,001 bytes of persisted map value**
and **29 bytes of metadata key**, totaling **338,030 logical metadata bytes**.
The test persists 1,000 boundary receipts with 32-byte group and row IDs,
without allocating 500,000 row images. This measures actual stored metadata
keys/values, not SQLite file-page allocation or filesystem overhead.

p04 and `unknown:false`. Each store held **2** unheld old puts.

## 2026-09-17 — W13gR1: current acquisition, readable floors and ordered snapshot pages

Base: `2a3cf84ed2ca067040eb1dd02c40f91848e5f03d`. This is the review round of
W13g, answering the six findings in the lane brief. No commit, push, publication,
ceiling increase, value-model change, existing corpus edit, agent delegation or
remote execution. The two preceding W13g entries remain historical records;
the selected historical floor described there is no longer a viewer wire value.

**Re-acquisition.** Chose the brief's option (b). A streamed acquisition of a
`delivered-history` group with earlier acquisition/history stays `unknown` on
its horizon index until a full replacement snapshot acquires it. This is
conservative and requires no per-row stamps. A missed deletion or a key that
moved below the new selection cannot turn an old retained image into a certified
current row. Point reads and incomplete local history still retain those images;
an unknown local answer can include them, while the online client falls back
for the held group. A full snapshot replaces held groups and restores coverage.
Continuous renewal preserves the existing boundary. The renewal regression now
also reads downward into its old retained rows and asserts unknown/incomplete.
There is still no eviction or backfill to maintain exactly N rows.

**Wire semantics.** The `acquisitions` shape and marker positions are unchanged.
A keyed join completion now carries the oldest *delivered current readable*
selected key at or above the private selection floor. Historical selection keys
stay private. Moving the former floor below its old selection, deleting it, or
moving it into an unreadable group narrows the public floor; both 800/2000
histories now have identical payloads again. If no safe selected key is delivered,
there is no completion, so the group stays unknown. An originally empty group
can still complete `whole`; whole-group acquisitions with surviving delivered
images keep `whole`. Snapshot replies additionally echo the request's `after`
cursor. The device persists the expected `next`, rejects mismatched continuations
before staging their rows or markers, and requires the terminal snapshot page
before catch-up can publish anything. A first page followed by the last page is
refused on both native stores and wasm; applying the actual middle page and then
the last page succeeds. A legacy snapshot without `acquisitions` leaves newly
acquired horizon groups unknown, not locally complete under an old count rule.

**Budget and storage.** Snapshot room now charges at least one unit per visited
group, including an empty one. The 5,000-group witness uses 434-character keys
(430 four-byte characters plus a four-digit prefix), so the base's limit-1
response really exceeds 16 MiB without violating the portable index-key cap.
It completes in **158 pages**: first limit 1, then limit 32. The largest marker
array is **114,369 bytes** and largest full HTTP response **119,311 bytes**.
The response ceiling remains **16,777,216 bytes**.

Boundaries are individually addressed under `device:acquisition-boundaries:`
and `device:snapshot:boundaries:`. Reads/predictions load their namespace once;
page application lazily fetches only the groups it touches, and saves only
changed entries. Namespace reset/removal is transactional on both stores,
including schema installation, store replacement, clear and snapshot publication.
The small core `store/activation.rs` change is necessary to clear these entries
inside backend installation's existing transaction. There is no compatibility
shim for the earlier on-disk map. At 1,000 groups of the previous `last 500`
measurement, floors still occupy **114,000 raw / 228,000 hex bytes**; independently
addressed metadata totals **356,000 key-and-value bytes**, versus **338,030** for
the old map, an increase of **17,970 bytes**. This is logical metadata size,
not SQLite page allocation. The hex floor is still twice its necessary raw
size; a later shrink can persist trailing components only.

The actual 1,000-lane merge makes **1,001** horizon scans (1,000 initial lanes
plus one refill). The base boundary implementation parses the whole map
**1,001 times**; the replacement parses it **0 times**, with **1 namespace load**
for the read. The before measurement temporarily restored the exact base versions
of `device.rs`, `boundary.rs`, `history.rs`, `predictions.rs`, `snapshot.rs` and
`partition.rs`, then restored the intended edits in a `finally` block. A counting
store wrapper observes metadata reads without changing the interpreter. Ordinary
pages now load no whole boundary namespace and persist no boundary entries;
changing one group persists one entry. The first passing wasm empty-group run
took **172,168.7575 ms** on this loaded host; that exposed the remaining whole
namespace reads during application and prompted the lazy per-group edit cache.
The read cache and changed-entry behavior, rather than a timing threshold, are
asserted by the regression.

The published sync card and README now state the boundary rule after a leave,
including `whole`, unknown retained re-acquisition, and legacy reply behavior.
`tests/device.rs` was split from **1,500** to **950** lines before its cursor
fixture edits; the moved tests are in `tests/device_scenarios/mod.rs`. The other
fixture edits only supply real continuations or update expectations for option
(b). No authoring form or diagnostic code was added. The shared wire comment,
TypeScript transport type, HTTP serializer and serializer tests follow the new
cursor echo; `engine/read.rs` needs no change because its existing unknown path
already withholds completeness.

As requested by the other reviewer, the preceding lane's wasm growth
(**+6,851 gzip bytes**, **474,456 total**, **7,456 above 467,000**) is recorded as
the cost of carrying acquisition metadata in wasm; it is not gated off. This
review round's final rebuilt artifact is **1,639,793 raw / 478,427 gzip bytes**,

unchanged report-only budget. The initial intermediate build was 1,638,501 raw /

## 2026-09-17 — W13gR2: completion presence is proved without a withheld floor

Base: `4886a043662a24ec03a81f2fb0c5fc1a0f061fd9`. This recheck closes the
remaining High: keeping a selected row's historical floor off the wire did
not stop that floor from deciding whether a completion appeared. The earlier
three W13g entries remain historical records. No commit, push, tag, publication,
remote execution, delegation, meter change or existing corpus edit.

**Implementation and wire semantics.** Join selection still uses
`group_at(join_seq)` and the same descending horizon sort and first N images.
The private selected floor is no longer computed or consulted. The rows
previously discarded by `truncate` are retained for this stream's proof.
The acquisition gathers the current readable selected keys actually delivered
between its markers. Its oldest delivered key K is safe unless an unselected
row still has its join-time key at or above K and is currently present,
readable and in this group. Such a row was never acquired. The highest such
falsifier is found first in the already descending unselected list; the next
delivered key above it is the narrowest safe completion. If none exists, only
the begin marker is published and the group remains unknown. No new index
scan is used. In the ordinary case the first unselected historical key is
below K, so the proof stops before any additional point read.

Chose the brief's conservative unchanged test: a same-key current readable
row counts as unchanged since the join even if a non-key write happened.
`PartitionRows` exposes no cheap per-row last-write sequence. A changed key,
deleted row or row outside the readable group cannot falsify the claim: the
post-join stream carries what happened to it at its own log position. Tests
also check completion on a limited stream page before that later write's page.
This can decline a provable boundary after a same-key write; it cannot certify
a missing unchanged row.

`acquisitions: [{ at, table, index, group, floor? }]`, its encoding, marker
positions and device handling are unchanged. A keyed `floor` now means the
oldest **provable** delivered current readable selected key, without the old
historical-floor eligibility condition. The paired histories publish p3's
1000 key in both worlds. The 1500 unselected-row control publishes p2's 2000
key; deleting p2 leaves no completion. A page ending exactly at or above the
published key is complete, while crossing it is unknown/incomplete on SQLite,
persisted memory and wasm. `whole` proves the same claim without a lower bound:
a selection of fewer than N rows has no unselected rows and can still publish
`whole` after all its selected rows become deleted or unreadable. This removes
the old requirement for a surviving selected image in that whole-group case.

**Leak argument.** The decision is a function of this stream's delivered
events (which the device receives) and current readable images (which it is
entitled to read), never the withheld selected floor. The history retained for
the proof identifies potential missing rows, but a row can block a completion
only through its own current readable image. Its key must equal the old key,
so any blocking ordering value is itself readable now. A withheld image does
not block the claim or supply a key. The two deletion histories and the two
move-into-unreadable-group histories, each with p3 moved from 3000 to 1000,
produce byte-identical viewer payloads. HTTP comparison excludes only the
independently generated `store_id`, as the existing two-world witness does.

The delivered **count** of a `last N` acquisition still depends on history when
a selected row is deleted or hidden before delivery. That is an existing
property of join-time selection, not repaired here. The lead's alternative of
selecting the current top N is left to the author; changing §18.2's selection
time is outside this lane. The code implements the requested conservative
proof; no contradictory behavior was found in the requested scenarios.

**Tests and measurement.** Added twelve regressions under `w13g_review/recheck.rs`
(six scenarios on each device store), and four wasm HTTP/device tests in
`horizon-boundary.test.mjs`. Existing W13g tests keep their meaning. The Rust
paired device payloads measure **591 bytes** (deletion) and **538 bytes**
(unreadable group), identically on both stores; each world emits **one**
completion at **1000**. The correctness control emits **one** at **2000**, or
**zero** when p2 is removed. Whole-group deletion/hide emits **one** `whole`.
There are **zero** added index scans, wire fields, diagnostic codes or notes.

## 2026-09-17 — W13gR3: a post-join write is a log fact, never an image comparison

Base: `0e7b9718f1073c93037ce30f0c502e4ee5008eb2`. This corrects the single
High in the second recheck. The W13gR2 entry above is a historical record:
its same-key shortcut and its leak argument are unsound and are superseded
by this entry. A p1 written away and back after the join was treated as an
unwritten blocker only when its withheld pre-join key equalled its current
key. The two worlds consequently differed in completion presence despite
identical selected rows, current images, and delivered events.

**Implementation.** `JoinSelection` now retains the join sequence.
`PartitionRows::written_after(table, id, seq) -> Result<bool, RuntimeError>`
asks whether this transaction's log contains any event for that table and id
strictly after the sequence. Both server implementations supply it: SQLite
and the Postgres evaluation adapter. The brief's implied per-row index did
not exist in either adapter; this change adds `_log_row_seq` on `(t, id, seq)`.
SQLite creates it with the existing store DDL. Postgres creates it at attach,
so both a new and a reopened evaluation store have the index.

The exact SQLite query is:

```sql
SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM _log WHERE t = ?1 AND id = ?2 AND seq > ?3)
```

The exact Postgres query is:

```sql
SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM _log WHERE t = $1 AND id = $2 AND seq > $3)
```

`join_completion` keeps the descending falsifier walk. The ordinary case
breaks when the first unselected key is below K, before any additional log
query or row fetch. A potential blocker with a post-join event is discharged
before fetching its current row; the old `index_key(current) != key` test is
deleted. A candidate with no such event proceeds through the existing current
presence, read-rule and group checks. The first real blocker narrows K to the
next delivered key above it, or to no completion. Join-time selection,
`whole`, the wire, `read.rs`, and device implementation are unchanged. Only
the blocker sentence changes in the README and sync card. There is no new
form, diagnostic, note, or diagnostic text.

**Corrected leak argument.** The completion decision is a function of the
delivered rows, the current readable images, and the post-join event set,
each of which the device receives. The historical descending list locates
potential blockers; a written row cannot block, regardless of whether its
current key happens to equal any withheld prior key. With no post-join write,
the join-time key is the row's current key. The remaining blocker therefore
uses a currently readable ordering value, with no equality or inequality test
between that row's current and historical images. This preserves the early
ordering stop without allowing a withheld key to decide completion presence.
As in the earlier lane, join-time selection itself is held fixed; this change
makes no broader claim that selection is independent of history.

**Regression and controls.** Four new Rust tests run the paired worlds and
same-key-only rewrite on SQLite and persisted memory. Two new wasm tests use
the real HTTP stream and wasm device. They assert that both p1 puts carry
1500, that the complete paired payloads including markers are byte-identical
(the independent HTTP `store_id` is excluded), that each completion is p3's
1000 key, and that the local two-row page is complete. Existing no-write
controls still narrow to 2000 or omit completion; the other W13g review and
probe tests retain their meaning, including the later-page write, key moves,
deletions, group moves, and `whole` controls. The additional core store test
checks strict `seq > join_seq`, table/id isolation, puts and deletes across
partitions, and the index plan. No existing corpus case was changed.

Measured payloads: Rust **755 B** for each paired world, **673 B** for the
same-key-only control; HTTP/wasm **769 B** and **679 B**, excluding `store_id`.
Each paired world has **2** post-join p1 puts, the same-key control **1**;
all have **1** completion at **1000**. The unwritten controls have **1** at
**2000**, or **0** when p2 is removed. The full wasm file's 5,000 empty groups
still take **158** pages with maximum response **119,311 B**.

**Query cost.** The new query is one indexed existence probe per potential
blocker on the rare path, independent of the number of other rows or the
number of events returned on this stream page. It stops at the first matching
entry and reads no image. The ordinary early-stop path adds **0** queries and
**0** fetches; a discharged candidate adds **1** log query and **0** row
fetches. With **10,004** logged events, SQLite reports **0** full-scan steps
for either outcome, **22** VM steps for a hit and **19** for a miss:

```text
SEARCH _log USING COVERING INDEX _log_row_seq (t=? AND id=? AND seq>?)
```

The cost model is O(log L) per candidate, at worst O(U log L) for U examined
unselected candidates, plus the existing current-row/rule checks only for
unwritten candidates. Postgres adds one database query for each probe; its
adapter is compile-checked here, not runtime-qualified against a live
Postgres cluster. The added index maintains one entry per log event and has
a one-time build cost when opening a store that lacks it. No meter ceiling
or resource policy was changed.
