## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 6: Grok's exact races and composed authority

Audited round 5 against Grok's additional details. No production change was
needed: verified replacement resets the floor/cursor and query epoch even at
the same head and generation; mutation receipts advance the floor with max;
close resets the last subscriber's watch and fetch checks its revision both
after receiving the result and after retry backoff.

The lower-head suggestion is scoped to verified replacement, preserving the
round 5 E_STORE_RESTORE rule for a same-store head below its dispatch-time
floor. Blindly lowering on any smaller head would weaken the write fence:
acknowledge revoke at S=10, then deliver an older same-store change head at
S=1 and a private query result at S=1. Lowering the floor would publish the
revoked row as fresh. A head captured before the write is therefore ignored
for lowering; a proven same-store regression refuses. Existing tests for both
cases and replacement A/100 -> B/1 passed. This is the only qualification of
Grok's proposed wording; the established authorization contract stays intact.

packages/snapback4/test/online-store-order.test.mjs adds four tests:
- Replace A/10 with B/10 at the same generation while both a direct query and
  a watch response are held. Neither old-store answer may publish as fresh.
- Replay an older mutation acknowledgement (S=1 after S=10), separately for
  direct queries and observations. The older query answer must be refetched;
  the replay must not lower the floor or reopen the revocation window.
- Close the final subscriber while a stale S=1 HTTP body is still in flight
  behind floor S=2, then release the body. Snapshot stays loading and there
  is exactly one query request. The existing deterministic backoff reset test
  separately covers cancellation after the yield.

packages/snapback4/test/composed-authority.test.mjs adds four real-server
tests: watch/query crossed with WASM/process SQLite devices. The fixture
acquires two scopes, leaves a delivered-history scope, and composes its one
retained row with two server-authorized private rows beyond a one-row device
horizon. It holds the second device reply after HTTP settlement and server()'s
authority check. A real membership revocation and sync then remove the private
rows, without changing store identity or schema generation. Releasing the old
device reply must publish no old server field, even transiently, while keeping
the authorized retained history. A direct device query proves the revocation
was applied before the held reply is released.

The exact surviving mutation is now caught: deleting only the authority
comparisons in runLocal and rerun, while keeping server()'s comparison intact,
fails both composed watch tests with secrets-2 AND the server-only secrets-1
in their publication traces. Five further mutation variants were caught:
ignoring same-head store changes, omitting replacement's queryEpoch increment,
letting a replay lower the floor, omitting close's reset, and omitting the
cancellation check after retry backoff. No mutation survived; generated files
were restored before the final validation.

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 7: store replacement terminates the online client

Round 7 supersedes round 5's cross-store reconciliation. The old online client
only verified identities through poll/probe heads, so direct queries could keep
retrying below the old floor; a replacement-store mutation receipt could lose
its fence; and an in-flight write could schedule another attempt after a
restore refusal. Store identity is now checked before receipt sequences or
query publications, and replacement or regression permanently ends that client.

File by file:

- crates/snapback4/src/serve.rs includes the evaluated reader's store_id in ready,
  unavailable and refused query replies, and store_id plus the current head in
  original/replayed mutation receipts and authenticated validation refusals.
  Identity/head metadata comes from one read snapshot on the operation's owner;
  its shared engine lock is released before the HTTP response is written. Query
  data, the legacy unavailable placeholder and release meter omission are unchanged.
- packages/snapback4/src/client.ts replaces rebasing, store epochs and head
  re-verification with one terminal transition. E_STORE_REPLACED or
  E_STORE_RESTORE fences all observations, aborts transport, settles every queued
  and in-flight write as failed/unknown, cancels retries, and guards later calls.
  Within-store monotonic reads, bounded refetches and close cancellation remain.
  Refusal replies' head participates in the read floor as well as query seq.
- packages/snapback4/src/app.ts reopens only the online tier on E_STORE_REPLACED,
  using the existing serialized auth ownership and persistence fences. It retires
  outstanding intents before closing/reopening, verifies the kept session on the
  replacement, republishes the client, and cancels verification on logout/close.
  E_STORE_RESTORE remains terminal and requires explicit recovery.
- packages/snapback4/src/app-online.ts fences durable admissions and retires the
  whole outbox, including an intent awaiting its admission write before raw
  dispatch; no automatic reopen or later restart replays those failed intents.
  Retirement also runs if another auth operation already superseded that owner.
- packages/snapback4/src/writes.ts preserves the unknown-execution warning in
  redacted terminal receipts; app-online.ts does the same for durable receipts.
- packages/snapback4/src/contract.ts, packages/snapback4/CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md
  and crates/snapback4-lang/src/guide/reads.rs document the narrowed terminal
  behavior. guide/sync.rs explains recovery and distinguishes local restoration;
  guide/codes.rs registers E_STORE_REPLACED and updates E_STORE_RESTORE;
  crates/snapback4-lang/src/diag.rs routes both codes to their dedicated sync text.
- crates/snapback4/tests/serve_store/mod.rs is a new real HTTP test on memory and
  pooled SQLite stores: ready/refused/validation query bodies, new/failed/replayed
  mutation receipts, identical identity across endpoints, and historical replay
  seq versus current head. serve_tests.rs registers it and checks identity on
  unavailable replies in dev/release. tests/serve_timeline/mod.rs validates and
  removes only each fixture's random store_id before its paired disclosure test.
- packages/snapback4/test/online-store-terminal.test.mjs adds 15 regressions:
  query/mutation/change/probe replacement and regression (eight); direct-only
  ready/unavailable/denied replacement (three); B/2 revocation with buffered B/1
  private data; same-head/same-generation replacement; historical replay head;
  and a buffered refusal preceding a newer grant. The matrix also checks new,
  queued and in-flight writes, immediate settlement before body release, exactly
  one terminal event, no retry, and no later HTTP request.
- packages/snapback4/test/app-store-replacement.test.mjs adds four regressions:
  replacement accepting/rejecting the session, plus logout/close during recovery.
  Admission of a second durable intent is paused across replacement; its receipt
  is failed and the queue is empty before reopening, with no resend after restart.
- packages/snapback4/test/online-store-order.test.mjs removes five superseded
  reconciliation expectations. The new terminal tests cover their replacement
  races; replay floors, stale-response bounds, initial identity and owner-close
  tests remain. client-seams.test.mjs, write-authority.test.mjs and
  write-ids.test.mjs assert the expanded wire envelope while preserving the public
  Write shape, historical-result withholding, and paired disclosure checks.

No new Quarry form or Read variant was introduced. Existing forms compile/run:
query page() returns [1], mutation change() returns 1, and the private-row
revocation fixtures still run. API examples: client.query(page, {}) on A/100
then B/1 returns denied E_STORE_REPLACED; A/100 then A/1 returns
E_STORE_RESTORE. A racing client.mutate(revoke, {}) returns failed with that
code, even if its receipt later arrives. createApp({ url, sessionStore }) opens
another client after replacement and keeps a session accepted by the new store.

Engineering decisions where the brief was silent: first authenticated response
identity binds the client; an actual regression compares its head with the floor
at request dispatch, so a buffered response preceding a later write is refetched
rather than falsely classified as restoration. Replay uses a separate current
head because its seq names a historical commit. Identity-less legacy replies
remain compatible; identity detection on direct queries/receipts requires the
updated server envelope. A store-change callback connects createClient to the
app owner without changing Client or Read. Retirement must persist before app
reopening; persistence failure reports an error and prevents that automatic reopen.

assets.ts snapshots mutable upload inputs into an owned Uint8Array and sends
that view directly. The installed React Native BlobManager rejects buffer
parts, while convertRequestBody accepts buffer views; wrapping the snapshot
in a Blob was the regression. ArrayBuffer.isView recognizes foreign views,
and the ArrayBuffer tag recognizes foreign buffers. Only the selected view
range is copied, once before the first request. Existing Blob inputs still
pass through without transferring their ownership. CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md

keeps the core open until receipt persistence and any deletion finish; its
finally releases that stage even if a device operation throws. The old

identity without declaring a restore, but cannot lower the receipt's floor. A
subsequent same-store head below that receipt is terminal E_STORE_RESTORE.

### 2026-09-24 — LLP 3000.013 lane E round 11: refusal fencing and I1–I7

Fixed all three round-10 review findings. A known server refusal conditionally
commits a tombstone for its still-stored bearer, preserving a different stored
successor; later offline restoration opens no replica. Epoch observation fences
all older scopes, including rollback candidates, before notification. Global
logout waits for the current rotation and privately retains the latest retry
credential in a backend-bound tombstone/journal until logout-all is acknowledged.
Ordinary retirement cannot consume it. Failed acknowledgement cleanup retries
locally, including on close. Client notifications and public client close now
keep auth state, viewer and client coherent. Updated the client reference and
LLP section 6 with I1–I7 and their assumptions. No public export was added.

The black-box three-runtime model now runs 5,000 seeds (130,000 commands), adding
logoutEverywhere, external server revocation followed by query/refresh, held
storage sets, offline reopen and public client close. It holds server-committed
responses and injects indexed get/set/delete failures, checks I1–I7 at store,
wire, auth/client callback and quiescent boundaries, and minimizes failures.
The standalone and full-suite runs produced identical coverage: 3,487 get,
356 set and 94 delete faults; 4,630 held writes with 24,723 peer commands while
storage was held; 4,773 external revocations and 9,007 offline fetches. Thirteen
reduced fixed cases and the 120-point failure sweep also pass. Fourteen focused
cases cover real online/local refusal, rollback, global logout/restart,
unpersisted successors, notification/close coherence and backend-bound custody.

Beyond the incoming findings, the model found refusal-fence transient failure,
refusal cleanup blocked by held sign-in, queued global revision supersession,
closed auth revision changes, ownerless global retry stuck restoring, late
refusal publishing restoring after close, failed acknowledgement deletion
retrying a consumed token, epoch retirement callbacks preceding view hiding,
and acknowledgement loss on close after failed cleanup read. Each is fixed
and retained as a reduced case. I6 probes additionally found early credential-loss
notifications and public-client close leaving signed-in auth. A model-inspired
real-server probe found global logout comparing an unpersisted successor instead
of its last kept bearer. Those also have regressions. The report records oracle
refinements and concrete counterexamples.

Measured: 219 affected tests and 15 model tests passed. Six negative controls
fail when refusal fencing, all-scope fencing, rotation waiting, notification
hiding, app-owned close or acknowledged cleanup is disabled. Both Chromium
witnesses pass: separate-tab session locking (740 ms), and shell/replica/account
offline reload with both servers stopped (1,617 ms). Reference check reports
504 LLP docs, 9,235 refs, zero errors/unchecked; whitespace check passes. The
single full scripts/test.sh run reports **`== 0 failure(s) in 148 s`**, exit 0:
all Rust groups pass, nine fixture passes, 1,157 client passes and 10 skips.
Development failures were ours and fixed, including a redundant schema refusal
handler that suppressed stale-restoration retries; no baseline/environmental
failure was waived. README stays 296/300 lines; local.ts is 1,479 lines.

Stopped the impossible unconditional extension of I7: if all refusal-tombstone
writes fail, every informed runtime dies, and reopening is offline, the old
bytes cannot be distinguished from a valid offline session. The informed runtime
denies access and reports the error; stronger crash exclusion needs durable
server evidence. Round 10's unknown-successor I3 limit remains. Lost global
revocation acknowledgements also need recoverable server receipts; E_AUTH alone
cannot prove all other sessions were revoked, so retry custody is retained.

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 9: terminal return fences and durable retirement model

Closed both Astra Highs. A direct online query could pass fetch's acceptance
check, then return its captured ready value after another response terminated
the client. client.query now rechecks store refusal, close/credentials and the
sequence/epoch fence immediately after await. A stale result becomes loading;
this outer boundary starts no additional retry loop. Observations also recheck
the result before installing metadata or expiry work, clear an invalid result,
and preserve terminal denial.

The durable-write race was in onlineCustody: createApp's synchronous hide paused
the owner, so active && terminal(result) skipped persistence. Its other return
path could refuse just-admitted work before the separately queued retirement
saved. Custody now owns one retirement promise. Admitted dispatch, admission,
and repeated-id refusal paths await it even after pause; a failed save returns
pending. Ordinary terminal settlement also persists independently of active UI
ownership. Retirement is idempotent. Automatic app reopening still waits for
retirement, and a persistence failure prevents that recovery from proceeding.

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 10: terminal entry points and refresh custody

Implemented Grok's remaining online-client findings on top of round 9.

may validate on its new client. Actions return the store refusal rather than
retryable pending; uploads and asset reads refuse before dispatch and after
awaits, and late asset handles are released. `assetSource` returns an empty

abort signal through both asset transports. `src/auth.ts` does the same for

continuation. A late successor this owner cannot keep is revoked once;
ordinary close keeps its existing in-flight rotation custody through a separate
client-owned refresh abort controller. Store refusal and credential loss abort
that controller immediately; ordinary close waits for custody. Sign-out cleanup
now shares this per-rotation owner instead of a second cleanup callback.

settlement and bulk store retirement: unknown E_STORE_REPLACED/E_STORE_RESTORE

was raised. `CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md` records terminal connectivity, entry-point

seed mutation an explicit null return: it writes different tables on its
two branches and does not use their implicit result. These are deliberate
updates to expectations that contradict the new refusal contract.

Engineering interpretations and limits:
- Null remains absence, adding optionality without a competing row kind;
  a zero-length sequence supplies no element to join. Treating these as
  conflicting row kinds would break ordinary nullable flow refinement and
  empty collectors. Both cases are documented/tested. This is the explicit
  compatibility interpretation of the brief's non-row restriction.
- Raw rows from different tables are also refused: their prior join was
  Unknown, which would violate the requirement that no row be erased.
  WriteRow is included in the safeguard for the same reason.
- A row/scalar mix cannot have a direct-spread answer for its scalar arm
  (`{ ...1 }` has no fields). Its rewrite explicitly projects row fields,
  wraps both whole results in `{ value: ... }`, and instructs the caller to
  read `.value`. That result-shape choice may require downstream edits;
  each subsequent independent incompatible join is still refused.
- A plain Object/row rewrite uses explicit plain-object projections. The
  diagnostic states that these do not copy pending metadata; row/row
  rewrites use spreads and retain it. This avoids inventing a row source
  for a plain object. The confirmed-row matrix proves data parity.

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 11: keep custody of committed network effects

Supersedes round 10's refresh/upload cancellation policy. The server can commit
old -> next before the refresh body is read; aborting that body converted the
rotation into E_OFFLINE, so cleanup saw no successor and logout could revoke
only old. The real-fetch/SQLite regression failed before this change: next
remained live after sign-out. The other reproduction submitted one durable id
twice before replacement; failed retirement left the first caller pending but
the overlapping recovery returned E_WRITE_RECEIPT_EXPIRED. Both are fixed.

Files and behavior (under packages/snapback4):

- src/request-wait.ts separates cancelling a caller from cancelling transport,
  and consumes local POST replies after the caller leaves. It extracts that
  work to keep local.ts under the 1,500-line limit (1,498 lines).
- src/client.ts never aborts mutation/action/upload/refresh requests. Public
  waits end on terminal refusal/close; refresh waits end on sign-out or terminal
  refusal, and the background rotation revokes an unkept successor exactly
  once. Ordinary close still keeps its existing refresh custody for restoration.
  Queries, probes, polls and asset GETs retain network cancellation. Late effect
  replies cannot publish, adopt credentials or retry against the replacement.
- src/auth.ts removes refresh's abort input and makes logout's existing deadline
  cancel only its wait. Login/signup/guest already sent without an abort signal.
  src/assets.ts removes upload's abort input; fetched assets remain cancellable.
- src/app.ts cancels superseded login/signup/guest waits without blocking later
  auth operations, consumes their background replies and revokes unkept bearers.
  Closing an opener also revokes a newly minted bearer that was never kept.
  Restoration of an already-kept session retains ordinary-close semantics.
- src/app-online.ts checks terminal refusal before and after duplicate receipt
  recovery, so every caller awaits retirement and reports pending on a failed
  save. Paused custody is also pending, rather than proof of receipt expiry.
- src/local.ts applies the same no-abort rule to effectful POSTs and cancels
  upload callers without adopting late facts. This is the shared transport for
  Node SQLite, web and native hosts. Local refresh and the web keepalive sender
  already preserved their effectful requests. App schema/recovery cancellation
  remains confined to read requests; no worker execution policy was changed.
- CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md documents the rule and unplaced cancelled uploads.

Tests and model:

- test/app.test.mjs adds the real SQLite server/real fetch unread-refresh-body
  reproduction for sign-out and replacement, verifying next is revoked and
  cancellation ends the public wait; it also covers local mutation/upload
  close, background response consumption and absence of late upload adoption.
- test/app-store-replacement.test.mjs submits a duplicate BEFORE replacement,
  alongside the existing after-replacement retry, through blocked and failing
  retirement saves. Neither caller may outrun persistence.
- test/effectful-cancellation.test.mjs uses actual HTTP/fetch with committed
  effects and held response bodies. Nine cases cover mutation/action/upload
  across sign-out, replacement and close, plus login/guest across logout,
  close and replacement; every minted bearer is kept or revoked.
- test/online-terminal-entrypoints.test.mjs changes round 10's deliberately
  superseded abort expectations: only the asset GET aborts, while effectful
  public waits end before their bodies arrive. test/online-store-terminal.test.mjs,
  test/page-ready.test.mjs and test/fixtures/page-observation.mjs allow held
  effectful requests without an AbortSignal.
- test/client-lifecycle.test.mjs now proves a mutation committed on the real
  server finishes delivery after close cancels its caller; no new write is
  admitted. Its fallback-count tests await startup sync so an authority reset
  cannot legitimately force a second read in a test measuring fallback routing.
- test/helpers/online-client-model.mjs and test/online-client-model.test.mjs add
  held login/guest responses, duplicate ids, body cancellation that rejects the
  unread body without rolling back its server effect, and R5. After fair drain,

  Client/app instances own their HTTP adapters; restoration traffic is kept

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 12: retirement survives receipt eviction

The round-10 helper discarded unknown store-failure receipts before sent
receipts, including failures just moved out of pending. With 256 sent receipts,
a replacement could clear the pending charge and its only receipt in the same
save. The reopened client then treated its id as new. The full-journal
regression now retries the retired charge itself, not a retained sent id.

Files and behavior:

- packages/snapback4/src/app-journal.ts owns receipt retention. Newly retired
  bodies are pinned; older unknown store outcomes compact to ids before the
  oldest ordinary receipts leave the unchanged 256-body window. Bulk retirement
  larger than that window also preserves every omitted failure id. Optional
  journal fields preserve compatibility with existing journals.
- packages/snapback4/src/app-online.ts uses that policy for settle and bulk
  retirement, coalesces the raw client's per-write store refusals into one
  queue retirement, and checks compact ids inside durable admission and receipt
  recovery. Another already-open owner cannot miss retirement by relying on
  its in-memory reservations.
- Compact retirement ids have no safe time expiry. They remain for this
  backend/account journal's lifetime, with a limit of 4,096 ids (about 116 KiB
  of serialized id strings, sixteen receipt windows). If another id cannot fit,
  the same atomic save sets a permanent retirementFull flag: new admissions
  refuse E_WRITE_RECEIPT_EXPIRED instead of dropping replay protection. Existing
  receipt bodies and admitted intents remain recoverable. Ordinary sent
  receipts retain the existing bounded window and do not consume compact-id
  capacity. Reconciliation and explicit journal replacement are required after
  saturation; neither sign-out nor reopening clears this protection. This bound
  is an engineering choice for rare unknown store outcomes, not a write-count
  limit on ordinary successful operations.
- packages/snapback4/src/client.ts also attempts best-effort logout of the
  known old bearer when an unkept refresh rejects with a retryable transport
  error: rejection does not prove rotation consumed it. No refreshAborter
  remains. Rotation never receives the read/request AbortSignal, so neither
  endCredentials nor stopForStore can abort it; a delivered successor is
  revoked rather than adopted. An unread successor genuinely lost by transport
  cannot be recovered by client code; old-bearer cleanup remains best effort,
  not a stronger server revocation claim.
- packages/snapback4/CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md and the writes guide card document
  compact ids, the cap, saturation, and the exception to reopening for receipt
  recovery. No Quarry syntax, public Read type, engine semantics or meters change.

Tests:

- test/app-store-replacement.test.mjs now retries newly retired ids after a
  journal with 256 sent receipts, and compacted old retirement ids with eight
  old unknown outcomes. None posts to the replacement; retained sent receipts
  still return their value-free confirmations.
- New test/app-retirement.test.mjs covers both store-failure codes through
  settle, 260 later successful settlements, reopening and another previously

  ids. Body eviction and the permanent admission fence are both reached.
- test/online-terminal-entrypoints.test.mjs adds sign-out and replacement with

- test/helpers/online-client-model.mjs and test/online-client-model.test.mjs add

## 2026-09-24 — LLP 3000.013 Lane K round 10: known-empty collectors and bounded diagnostic promises

Fixed the collector regression in types.rs: rebound preserves zero-length
List and Collection bounds, including under nested types. A reset to []
inside a loop no longer becomes an unbounded Unknown element that conflicts
with the next row append. Nonempty Unknown/row joins still refuse; no meter
or resource bound is removed. JoinError now records a field path through
objects, sequences and view projections. Differing outer object kinds also
check their shared fields for a deeper conflict, so an outer spread cannot
be suggested for a nested mismatch it would leave unresolved.

Removed the recursive diagnostic rewrite generator from
bind/program/joins.rs (198 lines before this round, 123 after). No more
collection-copy loops, scalar wrappers, recursive field projections,
source hoisting or generated temporary locals. Coalescing, nested conflicts,
containers, helper/operation returns, ordering helpers and complex source
expressions receive an explanation and an empty rewrite field. The message
names arm A and arm B's kinds, any conflicting field path, and the need to
make the kinds agree. diag.rs omits the rewrite line for that empty field;
the existing JSON field remains an empty string, with no envelope change.

Executable repairs are limited to flat row-derived locals or point reads
in a conditional or a two-value reassignment. The normalized types must
join, and assignment types must also be structurally assignable. The
condition and operands use the program's actual names. A nullable operand
is evaluated once with existing null-preserving shape/member behavior:
`((notes[key]) { rowCopy: { ... . } }).rowCopy`. This preserves absence and
pending while keeping each read at its original conditional or assignment
site. There is no temporary-name or eager-fallback setup to insert.

Engineering decision within the requested guarantee: assignment repairs
also require adjacent assignments, optionally with the second in a single
guarded branch whose condition does not use the assigned local. Otherwise
normalizing the initial RowShape to RowObject could change an intervening
wildcard shape before the conflicting assignment. Such cases get the same
explanation-only diagnostic. Scalar/plain-object arms also get explanations,
since spreading them cannot guarantee the common row kind or metadata.
Source operands retained by the binder are only for these located repairs,
not type-lattice or runtime provenance. No RowMixed machinery returned.

File-by-file integration: control.rs selects the conservative assignment
repair and locates append conflicts; expr.rs adds array element paths;
views.rs adds projected field paths. guide/codes.rs updates the existing
E_QUARRY_SHAPE_JOIN why entry; guide/shapes.rs states known emptiness and
which diagnostics promise source edits. sim/tests/common/shape_pages.rs
now checks explanation-only refusal for its incompatible record alternatives.
No new form or refusal code, no IR/device/wire/schema changes, and no
changes to authorization, disclosure, durability or metering behavior.

## 2026-09-24 — Lane J round 14: keep an unrotated bearer through store replacement

The refresh retirement continuation treated every retryable transport failure
as a reason to log out the old bearer. During store replacement, that bearer
is still owned by createApp's recovery probe; a refresh that never reached the
server left it valid, so cleanup could revoke the very session recovery was
trying to keep. Old-bearer cleanup now requires ended credentials (sign-out).
A delivered, unkept successor is still revoked, and no effectful request is
aborted.

Changes, file by file:

- packages/snapback4/src/client.ts limits retryable-failure retirement to
  sign-out. Store refusal without a successor leaves the live bearer alone.
- packages/snapback4/CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md documents bearer preservation
  for the replacement probe and continued cleanup on sign-out.
- test/online-terminal-entrypoints.test.mjs changes the rejected-refresh
  replacement expectation to no logout, keeping the sign-out cleanup and
  committed-successor cancellation regressions intact.
- test/app.test.mjs adds a real-server recovery case: a held refresh rejects
  before reaching the server, a query detects replacement, and the recovery
  probe presents the original bearer and restores the signed-in app. Its
  SQLite close regression now reopens offline before releasing the committed
  reply, checks that the id remains known, then reopens online and verifies
  that the original id settles with exactly one application.
- test/helpers/online-client-model.mjs adds an unreached-refresh transport
  outcome and an oracle forbidding cleanup of the still-kept bearer during
  replacement. test/online-client-model.test.mjs adds named replacement and
  sign-out replays and requires random coverage of unrotated recovery probes.
- test/navigation-model.test.mjs extends the real wasm-device/server model
  with 32 seeded schedules: close before execution, after commit, or after
  reply delivery; one or two offline reopens; online recovery before or after
  the original reply. Each checks durable id custody before server repair,

`crates/snapback4-lang/src/bind/program/control.rs` now excludes returning
and unconditionally refusing branches from `Binding::declared`, using the
same four-way choice as the flow type: join both survivors, keep the sole
survivor, or keep the incoming declaration when neither survives. Thus an
initially null local may hold a spread object on a branch returning 1 and
a row shape on a branch returning 2 without a spurious shape-join refusal.

### 2026-09-24 — LLP 3000.013, Lane K round 12: ordered control outcomes

Replaced round 11's unsound `terminates()` scan. Its later-return search
could discard a nullable declaration after an earlier conditional break or
continue, allowing `return x + 1` to reach null at runtime. The binder's
other exit analysis is a possible-transfer scan for aggregate diagnostics,
not an every-path reachability proof, so it is not reused for typing.

File by file:
- `crates/snapback4-lang/src/bind/program/flow.rs` computes each IR block's
  outcome set: fall-through, break, continue and return/refusal. Only the
  fall-through paths execute the next statement; earlier transfers remain.
  Conditionals union their arms. Loops consume their own break/continue and
  conservatively retain a possibly empty/exhausted path. A block terminates
  only when its sole outcome is return/refusal. Ordinary unknown conditions
  keep both paths; the analysis does not attempt constant folding.
- `bind/program/control.rs` uses those outcomes for the flow type, field
  refinements and declared type; declarations on loop-transfer paths still
  feed the existing loop fixed point. It computes each arm once per join.
  `bind/program.rs` registers the new module. The old independent exit and
  termination scans are removed; the operation-end exit check shares the
  same outcome computation.
- `tests/joined_shapes.rs` extends the loop-transfer regression with both
  break and continue before each of return and unconditional refusal. All
  four combinations now refuse `x + 1` with E_QUARRY_TYPE at compile time.
  Nullable rewrite tests compare the complete independently expected row,
  including id, title and owner, for every present arm.
- `tests/control_flow.rs` generates 2,048 bounded programs from four fixed
  random seeds using assignments, if, for, break, continue, return and
  require. A quarter emphasize nullable writes before competing exits.
  Every admitted program runs all eight boolean input combinations. The
  observed 1,110 clean programs produced 7,843 answers and 1,037 named STOP
  refusals, with no runtime E_TYPE; 938 programs were refused at compile
  time. Coverage assertions prevent an all-refused or all-returning pass.
  Two unit tests in flow.rs separately check statement ordering, unreachable
  tails, mixed outcomes, empty blocks and nested-loop transfer ownership.

## 2026-09-24 — a row born already expired is retired in its commit

This closes `issues/closed/20260923-snapback4-already-expired-grant-names-ids.md`.
The entry above left one case open. A row inserted with its lifetime already
over was later swept, and the sweep logged a `del` naming it and a scope
naming its group. The grantee never held either at a commit boundary.
Deciding at sweep time needed the principal's log history. I recommended
retiring such rows at the end of their own commit instead, and Charlie
approved it ("do it now"). The rule is in LLP 3000 §7.

**The change.** `Runner::retire_expired_births` runs at the end of every
program commit:

- `Engine::mutate`;
- job chunks;
- native job chunks;
- the Postgres adapter.

It removes each row born in the commit, in an expiring table, whose image is
expired at `now`. It uses the sweep's `remove`, so no rules apply, while
aggregates and events do. The rows are born, so their events are withdrawn
and a born grant logs no scope. A replacement beside a pre-commit
predecessor is not born, so it keeps the predecessor's owed scope. A row
revived to a live lifetime before the commit ends survives.

Retirement runs after the program's metering is recorded, under an unbounded
meter. The device's prediction does not retire. Seeds, loads and activation
are exempt and keep such rows for the sweep.

**Review.** Astra, blind (`llp/reviews/3000-retire-expired-births.astra.md`):

- **Round 1: NOT READY**, with no disclosure finding. It raised three
  problems:
  - **Medium, aggregate overflow.** Removal in id order could reach a sum
    total no commit held. The reproduction was a sum at `MAX`, then −1 and
    +1 born expired: retiring the −1 first overflows. Retirement now defers
    aggregate changes and applies one net change per target row.
  - **Medium, quadratic cost.** n expired siblings of one grant cost
    n(n−1)/2 replacement-scan visits, unmetered. Removing expired rows cannot
    change whether a key keeps a live row, so retirement memoizes it per
    key. 200 siblings now examine 199 rows, not 19,900.
  - **Low, expiring maintained table.** A raw schema could give a
    maintained table an `expire`, and retirement and the sweep would both be
    refused. The schema now refuses that shape.
- **Round 2: READY.** No new findings. Astra traced the memo's invariant: nothing
  reachable from the removal loop writes a live audience row. It traced the
  deferred aggregates, including keep-zero presence, mirrored columns and
  event order. It scanned 600 maintain declarations in the fixtures and
  found none with an expiring target.

**Mutation proof.** Each production hunk was disabled in the lane, its test
was run, and the file was restored byte-for-byte:

- **The memo: caught.** 19,900 rows examined.
- **Aggregate deferral: caught.** `E_OVERFLOW`.
- **The schema rule: caught.** The schema was admitted.
- **Retirement, in round 1: caught.** Disabling it fails the grant and
  content-row tests. Retiring every born row in an expiring table fails the
  revived-row guard.

**Rebase.** Main moved 123 commits during the work, including LLP 3000.013's
integration. `job.rs`'s chunk loop was restructured, and the call sits after
`check_final_exists` in the new loop.

**Verification.** Most runs were on `expo-build-450b`; the Mac was at load
80–100.

- **Full suite.** `run-rust-tests.mjs` ran all 858 targets on the rebased
  tree with the fixes, in 10.5 minutes. The four failures are the known
  environmental ones, with no `node_modules` on the host: the lang
  TypeScript typecheck tests and `check.rs` w11r1c.
- **An earlier red, before the rebase.** A run on the pre-rebase base
  showed five more failures: `schema_capabilities_legacy`,
  `uniform_word_expansion`, `census`, `application_fixture` and w9b. None
  touched the engine's write path. All five pass after the rebase:
  `application_fixture` needed the `benchmarks/fixtures` mirror, and main
  had fixed the rest.
- **Hot-path check, retirement on and off on the same host** (the lesson of
  `issues/closed/20260923-snapback4-born-row-tracking-is-quadratic.md`):

  | Target | Retirement on | Retirement off |
  |---|---|---|
  | `maintains::hidden_filter_work*` | 197.0 s, 195.0 s | 195.8 s, 195.5 s |
  | Clique `following_is_full_and_complete_at_the_envelope` | 17.6 s, 17.6 s | 17.7 s, 17.9 s |

  The device `following::calibration` measured 39.3 s in the full run.
- **Locally.** Core (84 lib tests and every integration target), sim
  `reviews` (30), `exhaustive`, `review_corrections`, `security` and

## 2026-09-24 — LLP 3000.015 Lane B2: engine-assigned `sequence by`

Implemented `ordinal: sequence by conversationId` as a required engine-owned
int. The binder validates the same-table parent reference, preserves redundant
explicit immutability, and supplies an index for bounded per-parent suffix
reads. `check` and column explanations name the parent counter. The types,
writes and language cards carry the form; the executable Clique recipe now
shares one conversation counter between messages and memberships instead of
accepting an application-supplied integer that can pin history forever.

The engine allocates across every declaring table/column inside the write's
transaction. Memory rows, in-memory/file SQLite and PostgreSQL have counter
storage; PostgreSQL uses the existing serialized-head/serializable retry
boundary, not a SQL SEQUENCE. Failed transactions, if-absent no-ops and write
retries consume no position. Deletion does not reuse a position; reopen
preserves the counter, explicit reset clears it, imports allocate omitted
ordinals and trusted restoration advances to the largest restored value.
Native and Quarry insert results include assigned fields. Device prediction
uses metered indexed suffixes across all declaring tables, including pending
rows and the settled image beneath a pending deletion. Predicted rows carry
pending, Write results remain pending, and settled images replace ordinals
and reorder pages. Device-only floor exhaustion queues through E_PREDICT.

E_SEQUENCE_PARENT and E_SEQUENCE_SUPPLIED have rewrites and explanations;
E_SEQUENCE_EXHAUSTED covers the positive int ceiling. The derived sequence-by
capability prevents older engines/devices from silently ignoring ownership.
Legacy Recorded markers infer only historical capabilities, so they cannot
substitute for the new capability carrier. Review found and closed device
floor budgeting, dropped-table import panic, and legacy-carrier bypass cases.
Full-suite upsert tests also caught a refactor regression; the original
preflight, double insert-rule accounting and collision disclosure are restored.

The smallest necessary extension to the spec is that the parent reference is
also immutable: moving an immutable ordinal 1 from parent A into parent B
already containing ordinal 1 would destroy the promised total order. Optional
parent references are refused. Multiple sequence columns in one row allocate
in column-name order. The checkout has no cap_count occupancy ledger; caps
use transaction-scoped index reads, so the new ledger follows the same write
transaction boundary. For populated-table addition/rebinding, the explicitly
allowed migration choice is E_ADOPT with an empty-table rewrite; there is no
implicit historical backfill. Empty tables may adopt the declaration.

Verification: nine focused core tests, three device tests covering both stores
online/offline, two language tests, the capability regressions and the tested
guide recipe pass. Real web and SQLite-backed clients prove two offline Write
results remain pending until settlement. PostgreSQL 16 tests pass in both
transaction modes, including four concurrent writers: 12 store tests and 18
corpus tests, zero failures. The optional test-postgres.sh experiment wrapper
stopped on its inherited stale experiments/postgres/Cargo.lock; the affected
core store and corpus commands ran directly without changing that lockfile.
The private PostgreSQL PIDs were recorded as 757126 and 891419; the first
exited during setup, and 891419 was stopped with a targeted SIGTERM and
confirmed shut down. Test harnesses manage their own recorded child handles.

## 2026-09-25 — LLP 3000.015 B1: field authority and private owner projection

Implemented `written by .principal` and `readable by audience` across
September 24–25 in Quarry,
schema IR and the shared engine. Supplied insert values require the named
owner; omissions use declared defaults. Each touched owned field uses the old
row's owner, while other fields use the ordinary row update grant. An owned
point patch needs no ordinary update grant, including when that grant probes
an online-only admin table. A named `update (old, next)` remains a transition
constraint; matching integer/time comparisons admit monotonic read marks.
Hidden targets and refused absent upserts retain NOT_FOUND; readable field
refusals use E_FIELD_AUTHORITY with an owner/default/visibility rewrite.

Private fields are removed from stored shared group/public images. Each
owner's principal partition also carries its projected row. Queries, scalar
selection, shapes, write results, snapshots, joins and refreshed stream images
respect the same visibility. Ownership transfer sends a tombstone, refreshed
to a redacted put only when the old viewer still reads the current row. This
normalization is limited to tables with private fields. Audience-only fields
keep ordinary projection heap cost. Private asset placements also constrain
asset download, preserving trusted system authority. Field ownership does
not grant row reading. Projection removes keys; selecting an absent private
field returns null, with optional TypeScript/Rust row types.

Device patches preserve another owner's missing contextual-default fields as
unknown. A transition depending on them, or acquiring their ownership, queues;
an independent owned-field patch still predicts. Capability fencing rejects
older consumers rather than silently dropping authority. Adoption treats
changed ownership/visibility as a rule generation change. check prints one
owner/visibility line per field; the rules and writes cards include Clique's
monotonic readUpTo/markRead recipe and a compiled language example.

Conservative boundaries beyond the brief: a field requires a declared default
and an ordinary required principal owner; nested written-by ownership refuses.
Private values cannot feed indexes/cursors, expiry, materialized aggregates,
recorded attribution or other rules' probes/non-update terms. The diagnostic
rewrites to readable by audience when that disclosure is intended. Local
named transitions remain supported; general cross-table ordered lookup was
not added. No store layout or wire protocol change, no PostgreSQL-specific
change, and no runtime meter ceiling increase.

## 2026-09-25 — Lane B2 review closure: exhaustion respects authority

The broader Grok review found one real boundary disclosure after the first
complete green run: a denied insert at an exhausted parent counter returned
E_SEQUENCE_EXHAUSTED before E_RULE (or NOT_FOUND for upsert). The new regression
failed with exactly that difference before the fix. A server allocation now
carries a sticky exhaustion flag and uses the last representable value only
as an authorization candidate. A denied writer gets the ordinary authority
refusal; an authorized exhausted attempt is refused before validation,
collision checks, asset work or persistence. No clamped row is published or
stored, and it cannot manufacture an if-absent collision. Authorized exhausted
if-absent attempts retain the prior E_SEQUENCE_EXHAUSTED behavior; ordinary
no-ops are unchanged. Imports refuse exhaustion immediately.

A device cannot decide server exhaustion from its held provisional suffix.
At the integer ceiling it now queues through E_PREDICT without publishing a
clamped image. The added memory/SQLite regression predicts one pending row
at I53_MAX and retains the next write unpredicted in the outbox. The writes
card documents this case. All ten core and four device sequence tests pass.

read, Serializable transactions retry the whole mutation on serialization

field with itself and the owner's tests. Finally, an ordinary patch retained
and metered another owner's private text at its actual length; precharge the
declared column copy bound instead. Owned/supplied values retain actual

## 2026-09-25 — 0.4.2 merged into the LLP 3000.015 baseline under one authorization law

Worked only in `snapback-sb5-land` on `sb5/land`, starting at `4bc28809db`,
under the author's no-push commission. `git fetch origin && git merge --no-ff
origin/main` brought `05382d59f0` (0.4.2: lanes U, Z, V, Y, X and T,
integration rounds 9–11, the three reverted commits staying reverted) onto
the B1/B2/B3 baseline. Forty-five files conflicted; every conflict was
resolved by reading both sides, and both designs are kept: 0.4.2's bounded
Following sources and event slots, its publication procedure and read-through
rules, the issued device clock and packed IndexedDB, and LLP 3000.015's field
authority, engine sequences, row-keyed views and their caller accounting law.
Read first: LLP 3000.015 §§1–3, LLP 3000.013 §13 on `origin/main`, the last
entries on each side and the two landing reviews.

**One law.** Every authorization-dependent scan or lookup 0.4.2 added or
changed now draws from the request-owned 8,192-candidate physical allowance
through the `Authorization` token and `GuardedRows`, and prices only
disclosed results after row and field authorization:

- `through.rs`: `capture_insert` fetches the parent through the token (its
  logical charges were prepaid by `reserve_capture`), evaluates the child's
  inherited read rule under `authorized_scratch` with a tokened `PrefixProbe`,
  and returns the stamped image as a sealed `Supplied` (`capture_input`, minted
  only there). `physical_children` reserves its schema-fixed examined/step/heap
  allowance and seeks every child table inside `authorized_scan`; it is what the
  expired-birth collision check, `retire_expired_births` and
  `sweep_server_rows` call. `refuse_live_children` does the same for its three
  seeks per child; the device's `current_children` reads the parent and scans
  children through the token under `device_work`, on the device's separate
  allowance.
- `through_read.rs`: `parent_verdict` fetches the parent through the token
  after its declared charges; `read_authority`, 0.4.2's three-valued parent
  verdict, is rebuilt on the same prepaid, restoring `authorized_scratch` scope
  as a provisional read (`rules::Verdict`, `ReadProbe` with its allowance);
  absence coverage goes through the tokened
  `authorization_absence_covered`; `captures_match` walks held children with
  the token.
- `read.rs`: `prefix_verdict` keeps 0.4.2's `(admitted, Pending)` contract and
  parent-pinned branch over our one prepaid scope; scan admission unions
  `parent_pinned`, `private_scan_authority`, `reserve_delivered_scan` and the
  private-page prepayment; the candidate loop keeps 0.4.2's kept-history rule
  under a denied parent and its provisional candidate deadline around the sealed
  `AuthorizedRow` pricing; `PrefixProbe` carries the allowance.
- `read_point.rs`: the point read is `authorized_point` (row and field
  authorization, then pricing) beneath 0.4.2's inherited-aggregate, parent-key
  and event-slot branches. A key rule's witnesses run as prepaid witnesses under
  the physical allowance even after its logical cut, and the cut stops the read
  before any aggregate state is fetched. A missing non-expiring inherited group
  authorizes its logical zero inside a restoring scope; a key-authorized
  parent-key image is sealed as a synthetic result (its fields are the caller's
  key and the disclosed total). An absent group answers `null`, which the
  compiled read coerces to zero; a denied one answers the unavailable object.
- `witness.rs`: 0.4.2's event-slot classification (a held source whose event
  kind is not fully synced is no witness; a miss past a partial read is
  unknown), aggregate-source dependencies and speculative notes live inside our
  bounded witness enumeration; lifetimes use `deadline()`/`expiry_column()`, so
  a read-through child's inherited deadline is one classification with
  `expire`.
- `live_aggregate.rs`: our row-keyed branch and tokened source scan ported into
  0.4.2's module; the point-scratch key price comes from the caller's evaluated
  key, never a stored image.
- `timeline/slots.rs` and `store/event_slots.rs`: the slot insertion copy is
  priced at the declared copy ceiling and the slot value as engine-minted; the
  activation fill reserves the declared ceiling on the adoption ledger. No
  raw `Value::heap_bytes` returns.
- `write.rs`: `reserve_capture` and `capture_insert` precede our independent
  insert denial and sequence preflight; the predecessor collision stays inside
  `authorized_scan`, followed by 0.4.2's expired-birth children check; event
  slots are prepared after `commit_sequences`; the cap check is B2's live-cap
  law with 0.4.2's `is_expiring()` classification (LLP 3000.013 §11.1's
  unswept rule stays superseded, as both LLPs record). `through_activation`'s
  adoption rewrites enter as system imports; its sweep scans through the token.

**Deadlines.** 0.4.2's scoped `Expiry` is the runner's type; B2's complete-rule
timeline runs on it through a frame-local `replace` that is detached outside
an emitting read (a write check owns no deadline, as 0.4.2 ruled), plus
`note_option` and `Pending::deadline`. Our save/restore sites became
scope/emit (`authorized_member`, `authorize_image`, `authorized_point`,
witness cache, row-view witnesses), a dropped scope (owner delivery) or a
deferred one (recount work records).

**Docs and fixtures.** LLPs are unions (LLP 3000 §7 gains this merge's

## 2026-09-26 — `guide receipts`: sent, delivered and read in one query

The Grok comparative on 0.4.1 charged receipts as three mechanisms where
Convex needed one query ("who has this ordinal?"). A new `receipts` card gives
the recipe. It uses two watermarks on each member's own row (`deliveredAt`,
`readAt`) and one helper, `receipt(m)`, which the history query returns with
every message. The recipient set is membership at send time. A member who
joined later is not a recipient, and a member who leaves drops out of messages
they had not reached. The client reports the newest fetched message's `at`, not
`now`, so a message committed after its last fetch stays `sent`.

Evidence:

- The card's block compiles clean, and `check` reports every operation as
  constant cost.
- A new engine test, `receipts_card_ticks_follow_the_recipient_set`, runs the
  card through sent → delivered → read, a leave, and a later join.
- A probe on the online, native and web tiers saw the sender's live history
  move within about 10 ms of each acknowledgement.
- Guide tests pass 84 of 84.

The language card, the operations doc's keyword line and the README's
reference map list the card. Aliases: receipt, delivered, read receipts, ticks,
watermark. The operations doc's alias example now says `sql` → from-sql; it
had said personas.

minute, with `fresh: true` and `complete: true`. The engine recorded no
dependency for `connected[p]`, and presence changes signal nothing. The 0.4.1
Grok comparative's builder had polled `memberPresence` from the client to work
around it.

- **Server.** A query evaluated on the server now names the principals it read
  and the bit it saw, as `presence: { p: bit }` beside its data. A held
  `/changes` poll takes `follow=p:bit,…`, at most 64 principals. It answers at
  once if a bit already differs. It also answers on a followed principal's
  first poll after its grace, and when a followed grace ends; a development
  clock advance wakes held polls for this. The answer carries each moved
  principal's new bit and keeps `seq` when only presence moved.
- **Clients.** Both clients keep the newest bit per principal and send the
  principals their live watches read. They restart a held poll whose follow list
  changed, and treat that as a restart, not a lost link. They re-run exactly the
  watches that read a moved principal.
- **Evidence.** Server tests cover every wake, the parser and the unchanged
  plain poll. A client test on the online, native and web tiers saw Alice's
  mark turn true about 20 ms after Bob started watching, and false about 1 s
  after Bob closed and the clock passed his grace.
- **Cost.** 719 B gzip on the web device (524,732 B), within the 525,000 B
  ratchet.

`NOT-DOING.md` keeps a presence API, last-seen storage and multi-server
presence out.

## 2026-09-26 — `guide receipts` round 1: ordinals, not the clock

Grok's review of the first card was NOT READY. Time watermarks tie at a
millisecond, cover messages the client never fetched, and accept any
`through`. The card now uses ordinals throughout:

- Every message takes the conversation's next ordinal, and a member records
  the last ordinal when they join. Commit order decides a message's
  recipients, including a join in the same millisecond as a send.
- A watermark is an ordinal. It only moves forward and never passes the last
  message (`PAST_LAST_MESSAGE`). `seen` writes only when it advances.
- A message with no recipients stays `sent`.
- `delete` is the member's own, via `leave`.
- The client snippet acknowledges only settled rows of a complete, fresh page,
  and lists `client` in its dependencies.
- The cost sentence says what `check --cost` certifies: one scan of at most 50
  member rows per message.

The card states one limit. A member who returns after more than the 500
synced messages acknowledges the newest ones, so older ones count as
delivered.

The engine test now commits m2 before anyone fetches m1. It covers a join in
the same millisecond as a send, a leave, a rejoin, a refused `through: 99`, a
backward acknowledgement and a conversation with no recipients. Six recipe
mutants each fail it:

- `<=` for joining;
- no bound on `through`;
- `read` with no recipients;
- storing the last ordinal instead of `through`;
- counting the sender;
- moving a watermark backward.

A probe on the online, native and web tiers moved sent → delivered → read
within about 20 ms of each acknowledgement. The readauth census lists the
card's ten entries.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence rounds 2–3: no lost wakes, and tokens instead of bits

Grok's first review, of the design before grants, was NOT READY, and so was
Astra's first, of the version with grants. Both found that the bits were a
disclosure, and each found wake races.

- **Opaque tokens.** A query now answers an opaque token bound to its viewer,
  and never the principals or bits. The bits behind an aggregate such as
  `connected[bob] + connected[carol]` stay on the server. A poll follows only
  its own viewer's tokens, answers only which of them moved, and drops a token
  that lapses mid-wait. Tokens replace grants, and remove the comma problem in
  principal names.
- **No lost wakes.** A presence generation moves under the change lock, so a
  wake between a poll's checks and its wait is never lost.
- **No spurious answers.** A presence wake answers only a poll whose tokens
  moved, so unrelated polls and absence-guarded pushes are undisturbed.
- **Consistent reads.** One run reads each principal once, so an answer's reads
  agree with its token.
- **Composed reads.** Composed local answers carry the server's token.

The server tests cover:

- a token that moves and answers;
- an already-moved token answering at once;
- a grace that ends on its own deadline (a test that deleting the deadline arm
  now fails);
- a bystander poll surviving presence wakes;
- a foreign or unknown token following nothing;
- an aggregate disclosing no principal;
- a lapsed token staying quiet.

The three-tier client test still turns Alice's mark true about 20 ms after Bob
connects.

## 2026-09-26 — `guide receipts` round 2: monotonic receipts, fetched runs only

Astra's review of the ordinal card (NOT READY) and Grok's round-1 delta review
(NOT READY) agreed on the remaining defects:

- A receipt could move backward when every recipient left.
- A watermark claimed messages the client never fetched: the top of a paged
  view, or anything behind the 500-message horizon.
- Offline viewing was never acknowledged.
- Pending sends rendered as accepted.

Now:

- **A receipt never moves backward.** A message records how many recipients it
  had. Once all of them leave, the requirement is met, while a message sent to
  nobody stays `sent`.
- **A watermark claims only fetched messages.** Both `delivered` and `seen`
  claim only an unbroken run of fetched messages after the member's delivered
  watermark. The client loads older pages to close any gap, which removes the
  500-message limit.
- **Offline viewing counts.** Acknowledgements need only a complete page, not a
  fresh one.
- **Pending rows render as pending,** not as `sent`.

The engine test adds three cases:

- the only recipient reading, then leaving, then rejoining;
- a refused `seen(99)`;
- sends to nobody.

Two new mutants each fail it: counting only remaining recipients, and an
unbounded `seen`. The three-tier probe still moves sent → delivered → read
within about 10 ms of each acknowledgement.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 4: a token stands for its query

Astra's third review was NOT READY and Grok's READY WITH CHANGES. Astra showed
that a token could still say more than its query: `connected[p] > 1` stayed
false while its token moved. A token also outlived its viewer's access, and the
token table had no byte bound. Both reviews found that a moved token was polled
in a loop while its watch re-ran, and that a full table stopped a watch's
renewal for good. Astra also found that a late presence notice could end a
bystander's poll.

- **A token stands for its query.** It keeps the query's name, arguments and
  viewer, and a digest of the answer it published. When a count it read moves,
  the poll re-runs the query as the viewer, and reports the token only if the
  digest changed. The baseline moves either way, so a change is reported once.
- **A token that no longer answers its viewer retires silently.** That happens
  when a commit since its answer touched a table it read, or when the re-run is
  refused.
- **A bounded table.** It holds 100,000 tokens, 64 MiB and 256 per viewer; the
  least recently followed token makes room. Following keeps a token live, and
  it lapses 120 s after the last follow. A lapsed, evicted or foreign token is
  reported at once, so its watch re-runs. The client's five-minute renewal is
  gone.
- **Clients** stop following a reported token until the re-run answers. An
  answer too large to follow carries an empty token, and its watch re-runs
  every 30 s.
- **Counts, not bits.** A second device, or one of two ending, moves
  `connected[p]`, and both wake followers.
- **Every wake is one more look.** The presence notice goes out under the
  change lock, and a poll answers only a change it sees.

Evidence: nine server tests, and eight server mutants that fail them; three
client tests on a controlled transport; the three-tier test, where Bob's mark
turns true in about 20 ms.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 5: a refresh, not a follow

Astra's fourth review of the follow design was NOT READY again. It found that
a clock-dependent answer such as `now + connected[p] * 0` reopened the
hidden-count oracle. Retiring a token made a revocation observable at a
presence change. Retained arguments outgrew their charge. And two clients
reading each other's connection counts fed each other's poll restarts, at 65
polls a second.

Four rounds had each closed their predecessor's defects and opened new ones.
Following presence exactly, without telling a client more than re-running its
query would, needs a double evaluation at one instant, delivery-latched
reports, conservative memory accounting and restart-free polling. For an
online mark that is too much surface, so round 5 ships the simple version:

- **An answer that read presence asks for its refresh.** The `/q/` reply
  carries `refresh: 5000`, and names no principal or count.
- **Clients re-run the watch every 5 seconds, keeping the answer.** The online
  client retains it, marked `fresh: false`, until the new answer arrives. The
  local tier publishes only the new answer. Closing a watch stops its refresh.
- **The server keeps nothing and wakes nothing.** The token table, follow
  lists, presence generation and count wakes are gone. The change poll is as it
  was in 0.4.2.

The once-per-run memoized presence read stays, so every read in one answer
agrees. Alice's mark now turns within about 5 seconds, on every tier, with no
loading in between. LLP 3000.018 §6 records the follow design and why it waits.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 6: the query asks, and the refresh waits its turn

Astra's review of the refresh was NOT READY, and Grok's found smaller gaps:

- **`refresh` disclosed a branch.** It came from the run's own reads, so
  `if flag.enabled: return connected[viewer] * 0` revealed the flag. Now the
  query decides, not the run: the binder's `presence` residency site, which
  already covers helpers. Rules cannot read `connected`. Every reply of such a
  query carries it, authored refusals included, so a query that is refused at
  first keeps refreshing.
- **A retained refresh outlived expiry and revocation.** The refresh is now a
  background one-shot read. It publishes only if nothing was published, and no
  other read began, while it ran. Expiry and invalidation withdraw at once, as
  before, and win.
- **The local tier flashed loading, and never stopped refreshing.** The
  background read touches no snapshot until it publishes. A served answer
  without `refresh` now stops it; a device answer keeps it.
- **Timers.** A dead session and a replaced store clear them. The client clamps
  an interval a timer cannot hold.
- **Smaller fixes.** The memo is heap-metered, the outcome's presence map is
  gone, and the Postgres feature builds again.

A composed test finally exercises the composed path: retained history beside
presence, on the wasm and process devices. Dropping the composed `refresh` copy
fails it.

## 2026-09-26 — Receipts card round 19: owed for the life of the client

Astra's round-18 review found a view the client could not keep lost when its

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 7: what a background reply may decide

Astra's review of round 6 confirmed the static decision and found five smaller
gaps, all in what a background reply may change:

- **An overtaken reply decides nothing.** It could clear the interval that a
  newer read had set. Now a reply that a publication or another read overtook
  touches neither the answer nor the timer.
- **An accepted loading answer publishes.** A query whose authoritative answer
  is loading no longer shows its previous value as fresh.
- **A background failure is quiet.** A 503 marked the link offline and
  withdrew answers. Background reads now use a quiet request that keeps the
  answer and the interval and retries; the change feed notices a real outage.
- **Eligibility comes from the evaluating schema.** It now comes from the
  engine or reader that runs the query, not the schema looked up before an
  adoption could land.
- **The contract says a presence answer is a sample.**

The per-run memo's heap charge moved the w15a meters by 67 bytes per guard read
outside the effect path, and the pins now name that charge.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 8: an overtaken reply remembers nothing

Astra's review of round 7 found one Medium and two Lows:

- **An overtaken reply rewrote the recovery cache.** The local client stored a
  background reply's answer as it settled, before asking whether a newer read
  had overtaken it. So a later outage recovered the discarded answer. A
  background read now writes through a staged cache. Its writes apply only when
  the reply is published, and only to entries no other read replaced
  meanwhile.
- **A read that settled after sign-out rearmed the timer.** Arming now consults
  the session itself, so no completion order can leave an interval behind.
- **`fresh` promised more than a sample gives.** The contract and the RFC now
  say a presence sample keeps the flag it arrived with until replaced, and that
  failures and suspension remove any bound on its age.

Round 7 also claimed the retained-row composition was unreachable for a
presence query. Astra reached it: a device evaluates `connected` as unknown, not
never. The read-through fixture now observes such a query and requires it to
keep refreshing. The local failure, loading and overtaken-reply cases now run on
the wasm and process devices, and an online case shows a background reply older
than an observed commit is never published.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 9: remembered answers in the order reads began

Both reviews of round 8 confirmed its three fixes; Astra reproduced the
session-death Low's fix with a timer barrier. They then found opposite faults
in the staged cache's guard, which compared entries by identity:

- **Astra:** a newer one-shot refusal deleted an answer that was never
  remembered, and the older background reply, accepted anyway, wrote it back.
- **Grok:** an older one-shot answer that landed while a refresh ran made the
  newer accepted reply skip its write, so recovery stepped backward.

Both are about order, so round 9 orders the remembered answers by when each
read began. Every read takes a ticket as it begins, and a write of a key,
deletions included, applies only if no read that began later has written it.
That also makes round 8's staging unnecessary: an overtaken reply can never
outrank the read that overtook it. So staging and its acceptance hook are gone.

The online client now gates its timer the way the local one does: ended
credentials keep no interval, whatever read settles last. The race lies
between a reply and its caller resuming, so no fake transport reaches it, and
the gate is structural. The RFC and the contract now say a composed sample
keeps the `fresh: false` it arrived with. New local cases: an accepted
background reply is what recovery shows, and it replaces an older one-shot
answer that landed while it ran; an older refusal landing later does not erase
it; and the accepted loading and refusal cases run through an outage.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 10: the server's cut orders what recovery remembers

Astra's review of round 9 confirmed its fixes and found request-start order
insufficient on its own. A one-shot read held before reaching the server, then
refused at a later store cut, lost to an earlier answer because its read began
first. A read retried after the store changed kept its first ticket, so it lost
to reads that began while it waited. Now a server's answer or refusal carries
the store cut it read (`seq`), and a remembered answer is replaced only by one
that is not older: a later cut wins, and at the same cut the attempt that began
later wins. Every evaluation attempt, a retry included, takes a new ticket.
Local cleanup of an expired or composed answer forgets it without changing the
order.

Astra also showed the online credentials gate was testable after all. A barrier
on the observation's fetch holds a completed read while a change-feed `E_AUTH`
ends the credentials, and a timer spy then sees no presence timer. The latency
bound in RFC §3.3 now counts the read in flight when presence changed.

Grok's review of round 9 was READY WITH CHANGES. It found the local-reads unit
test still treating the remembered answers as a map, so its assertions after the
first never ran; that test and the prediction-routing fakes now use the ordered
cache. A new local case shows that forgetting an expired answer, offline, leaves
the next server answer free to be remembered.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 11: a refusal names its own cut

Both reviews of round 10 found the store-cut order leaking in three places:

- A refusal was labeled with the store head taken before its query ran, so a
  commit in between made it look older than it was. The engine now returns
  the cut its query transaction read beside the result (`Engine::query_at`),
  and a refusal reply names it as `seq`.
- A refetch after the credentials changed, and an expired device answer
  re-routed to the server, reused the attempt's ticket. Each refetch now
  renews it.
- A reply with no cut was ordered as cut 0, so it could never replace a
  remembered answer. A missing cut is now unknown, and then only when the
  reads began decides.

The later-cut test now refuses with `head` alone, as older servers do. New
unit cases cover the order itself, both renewals through `evaluateLocal`, and
a reply without a cut. The prediction-routing tests run on the real cache.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 12: a cut once named stays known

Astra's round-11 review found two more ways an older reply could replace a
newer one, and a server test too weak to catch the round-10 defect:

- The order compared each reply only with the one remembered. A refusal at
  cut 8, then a loading reply with no cut, let an answer read at cut 7 win on
  its ticket. Each query now keeps the highest cut any reply has named, kept
  or not, and a reply below it is older. An answer remembered with a cut is
  therefore always at the highest cut named. A brute-force check of every
  arrival order of 20,000 small reply sets found no lower-cut answer
  remembered. Replies without a cut are still ordered only by their reads, so
  the final state can depend on arrival order.
- A composed read, which remembers no whole answer, erased memory
  unconditionally: its cleanup when it composed, and its reply when it
  arrived. Both are now ordered deletions, so a later read's answer stays.
- The server test required `seq == head` on an uncontended store, which the
  round-10 defect also satisfies. A test hook now commits between the reply's
  metadata and the query's own read, and the refusal must name the cut one
  past its head.

New client cases: Astra's three-reply schedule, a cut named by a reply that
lost on its ticket, both composed-read paths through `evaluateLocal`, and a
refusal carrying `seq` and an older `head`. Of nine mutants, one survived: a
composed read's whole answer could be remembered with no test noticing, a gap
older than this round. A case now requires that nothing is remembered.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 13: a composed answer is ordered too

Astra's round-12 review found the last path around the order. A composed

So an older answer that landed after it was remembered, and a later outage

Round 14 is a test. Astra's round-13 review (READY WITH CHANGES) found every
