## 2026-09-26 — The scale certificate separates a cleanup backlog from growth

Calibration #21's builder read `scale: 6 of 8 operations are constant; 2 grow
with data (home, cards)` on the paved Following program, and wrote that it was
not treating short functional tests as a scale proof. The two reads grow only
with a backlog: feed entries that an unfollow or a removal retired, which
background cleanup purges in chunks of at most 256. Expired rows the sweep has
not reached are the same kind of cost.

The certificate now has a third class, `backlog`, which reads
`constant once background cleanup catches up; until then at most N rows
examined: …`. It keeps the read meter's allowance, because a burst or downtime
can leave any backlog, and the summary counts it apart:
`2 constant once background cleanup catches up (home, cards); 0 grow with
data`. Only the scan the compiler generates for a timeline read qualifies:
its one filter is the platform's retirement check. A residual filter over
application data, a per-row read rule and a maintained aggregate over expiring
contributions still grow. `guide bounds` says so, and the pinned certificates
in the scale, expiry and Following tests moved with it.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 1: only the compiler's own timeline scan is a backlog

Both review families found the same High: the first cut trusted a table's
name. A scan of the owned feed table with a filter of its own
(`feedFeed[viewer] … where not .repost`) was called a backlog, though live
reposts survive cleanup. So was any application table whose name ended in
`Broadcast`, which is not even an owned suffix. Now the binder records the one
scan it generates when it expands a timeline read, and the certificate grants
`backlog` to that scan alone. An authored scan grows, even one that spells the
platform's check by hand. Without the binder's record there is no proof, and
the read grows too.

Inside a growing certificate a cleanup site now keeps its own words. Under a
condition whose only extra work is cleanup, it reads `constant once background
cleanup catches up (…)`. Beside real growth, it reads `also, until background
cleanup catches up, …`. The README and `guide bounds` describe three classes,
and apply `backlog` only when cleanup explains all of an operation's variable
work.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 2: the record names one scan

Both families found that round 1's record was ambient: it marked every scan of
the feed table bound while a timeline read expanded, including an authored scan
inside a helper in the read's own cursor or key. Such a read was certified
`backlog` although live reposts it skips survive cleanup. The binder now
records a scan only if it is the feed table read at the timeline read's own
source site, which only the generated scan is. Astra also found that a
condition's cleanup promise ignored unconditional growth; every variant now
takes at least the class of the work that runs in all of them. The summary
test now pins all three counts, and a test pins the guide's and README's
three-class wording.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 3: a variant answers for every site that can run with it

Both reviews of round 2 found that a condition's class still ignored growth
recorded under other conditions: a scan that grows whether `status` is present
or absent, or whatever `label` is, runs beside the variant where the assignee
is pinned, yet that variant still promised `constant once background cleanup
catches up`. Sites and variants now keep their presence conditions, and every
variant takes at least the class of each site whose conditions do not
contradict its own. Unconditional sites contradict nothing. New tests cover a
status-wide scan, an orthogonal input, a coarser variant beside a finer
growing site, and an unconditional expiring scan that makes otherwise
constant variants a backlog.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 4: conditions are bindings, not spellings

Astra's review of round 3 found conditions matched by the name the author
wrote. A helper's `assignee` parameter, called with the query's `a`, looked
like the query's own `assignee`, so a variant promised cleanup while the
helper's scan grew. And `selected = assignee` was treated as independent of
`assignee`. Conditions now carry the binding they test. A binding that only
copies another, and neither is ever reassigned, tests its source. Variants
merge by those bindings, and each reads under the name of the binding it
finally tests: the helper's parameter reads as `a`, and a copy of `status`
as `status`. A reassigned copy stays its own binding. New tests cover the
helper, the helper in a loop, the alias, a reassigned copy, two bindings
that share a spelling, and conditional cleanup beside constant variants.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 5: only an argument's presence defines a variant

Astra's review of round 4 found three more gaps. A loop variable, or a copy
reassigned in a loop, takes both values in one call, yet it was treated as a
fixed condition. Repeated searches of one argument got separate identities.
And an alias tested inside a test of its own source merged two contradictory
facts into one variant. Presence variants now come only from an argument's
presence, which is fixed for the whole call. A copy counts only if it is never
reassigned, and Quarry never reassigns an argument. A test of anything else
runs both ways, so its branches count as unconditional. A test that an
enclosing test already decided adds no fact, and its other branch is recorded
as unreachable. A searched argument is one condition however often it is
searched.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 6: what follows a returning branch

Astra (READY WITH CHANGES) and Grok (READY WITH CHANGES) reviewed round 5.
Astra asked for sharper tests of the nested case. The nested test now pins its
one variant and its one cleanup site, and a mirrored case checks the absent
branch. Grok found two more gaps:

- Code after a branch that returns was treated as running in every call. In
  `if assignee != null: return <pinned>` followed by `return <unpinned>`, the
  second scan runs only when the assignee is absent, yet it grew the present
  variant. The walk now covers the whole body at once. What follows a branch
  that leaves the body (`return`, `break`, `continue`) is analyzed in the
  other branch's case. When both branches leave, or the branch an enclosing
  test decided leaves, what follows never runs.
- One presence state could be spelled two ways when its tests nested in
  opposite orders. Condition names are now sorted, so `status and assignee`
  reads `assignee and status` everywhere.

Grok also named a surviving mutation: skipping expression blocks when
finding reassigned bindings. A new test covers it: `matching (needle ?? 'x')`
searches in every call, so it must not claim a constant absent case.

Ten mutants of the change fail the tests. Four of them needed a new test of
every way out of a body: both branches returning, `continue` in a loop, and
a nested test whose branches both return. Quarry accepts code after such a
test, so the certificate must not charge it.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 7: leaving, judged under the facts in force

Astra reviewed round 6 (READY WITH CHANGES). Deciding whether a branch leaves
its body was purely syntactic. A branch that returns through a nested test of
the same argument, `if assignee != null: if assignee != null: return …`, was
judged able to fall through, so what followed it was charged to every call. A
test's exit is now judged under the presence facts each branch runs with. A
decided nested test leaves exactly when its selected branch does. The
fall-through test also compares the work (rows, probes and lanes) with its
explicit-`else` twin, not only the classes: charging what follows at zero
iterations survived before.

Grok's review of round 6 (READY WITH CHANGES) found two more ways a scan that
never runs was charged, both making a backlog operation read as growing. A
`require` that no call can pass (`require false`, or two literals compared so
the comparison fails) now leaves as a `return` does. Nothing after a `return`,
`break`, `continue` or such a refusal in the same body is charged: it is
walked for its bindings and its rows still count toward the bounds, but it
adds no site. A loop whose body returns can run no times, so it never leaves.
A test now pins that, since treating it as leaving survived before.

One pessimism is left as it was in round 5: a helper that falls through after
a returning branch is lowered with a `$returned` flag, which is not a presence
test, so what follows is charged to every call. The README's certificate
paragraph fits its three lines again, within the README's 300-line budget.
Twelve mutants of rounds 6 and 7 fail the tests.

## 2026-09-26 — Live presence round 15: a composed read clears nothing before its reply

Grok's review of rounds 12 to 14 found every earlier finding fixed and one new
defect from round 12. That round turned a composed read's up-front cleanup into
an ordered deletion. The deletion named no cut, because the server had not
answered yet, so it took the order's place by its read's ticket alone. An
earlier read's answer at a higher cut, landing while the composed read was out,
was then turned away. The composed read's lower refusal was turned away too,
and nothing was remembered. Any cleanup before the reply is unordered: as a
forget it erases a newer answer, and as a deletion it blocks an older read's
higher cut. So the composed read now clears nothing up front. Its reply names
the server's cut and takes its place in the order, as it already did. A case
covers Grok's schedule: cut 100 lands during the composed read, which is then
refused at cut 40, and the cut-100 answer is kept. Two routing tests had pinned
the old erase: offline, a composed read left the cache empty. They now require
that it leave the cache as it was. A composed read still never recovers a whole
answer, and its reply, when one comes, takes its place in the order.

### 2026-09-25 — LLP 3000.017, E1 ephemeral tables

Implemented the compiler, core, engine, HTTP server and device boundary for
`ephemeral 1s` through `ephemeral 60s`. The exhaustive IR effects walk includes
expression blocks, helpers, loop domains and merge lanes; renewal keys account
for assignments across loop iterations. Generation admission independently
recomputes operation facts. The 26 valid existing language fixtures were captured
at base `59dc258fe5e06cec28ee65da5bfe1bae3f3c7509` before any implementation;
their schema JSON and emitted TypeScript remain byte-identical.

One shared hub holds rows, writer/declared-size accounting, an epoch, incarnation
and bounded ring under one mutex. A Layered Rows drop guard undoes every incomplete
write. Ephemeral execution uses a deferred durable read snapshot, rechecks insert
authority whenever it stamps a deadline, checks declared capacity before commit,
and creates no durable replay, log, commit, outbox or row. Only queries with
`ephemeralReads` lock the hub. Adoption clears memory; durable-to-ephemeral
activation deletes physical rows/index entries. Import/seed and Postgres refuse.

The HTTP lane precedes replay and has its own session token bucket. All route
refusals, including auth and input admission, are HTTP 200 failed. Polls use a
separate wake mutex/condition, interest filtering, 100 ms pacing, and independent
memory versions; an already-blocked poll finishes with the serving engine mutex
held. Presence reconnect checks are read-first. Server checkpoint
`4c1c8492c` passed 81 server tests (including nine ephemeral HTTP tests).
SERVER.md was updated before this checkpoint because it is under the E2-owned
package tree. No tracked package files are edited after it; the explicitly
required build/test scripts regenerate ignored wasm/build outputs there.

The guide's typing alias, separate chats-list hint, 10 s viewing heartbeat,
renewal law, timing bound and refusal table are executable examples. The old
reads-card 4.5 s durable typing example is replaced per RFC §2.5: its pinned
block hash, prose fact and test now follow the ephemeral card, and the language
card's new declaration and keyword list update their two explicit pins. Existing
durable schema/output fixtures were not changed. The card compile harness allows
only the new mandated N_EPHEMERAL_SERVER note for ephemeral examples. E2 owns the
README orientation line and the new TypeScript Ephemeral/Signal contracts; the
old README keyword-list test still identifies that pending cross-lane addition.
The React examples are additionally checked against the real Read union/current
React hooks with current mutation handles; the Ephemeral overload is E2's proof.

Small implementation choices where the RFC leaves mechanics open: a 256-entry
change ring; dev personas use their principal as the session bucket identity,
while bearer tokens use a digest; 4,096 idle-evicted bucket entries bound host
memory. Different store identities are unordered and require explicit replacement
rebind; a stale reader cannot rebind a new store back to the old one. The durable
read transaction is ended while the memory undo guard is still alive. Declared
capacity includes the bounded image plus each bounded index key, with no actual
private payload size input. Unstable loop keys conservatively disable renewal.
The chats-list hint uses a paged membership scan with a nested typing read, an
accepted alternative in RFC §2.3. The device refuses both ordinary and replay
admission before opening its writer transaction; reads stay unknown.

### 2026-09-25 — E1 final-suite corrections

The first E1 full suite also caught an introduced streaming-bearer regression:
the detached poll reader used `identity::resolve`, which attempts expired-session
cleanup on a missing credential. That made a revoked bearer report E_STORE from
the read-only SQLite connection. `resolve_read_only` shares the complete live
authority walk and omits only cleanup; ordinary writer-backed resolution is
unchanged. The original streaming client test now passes, and a new HTTP test
revokes a bearer, holds the engine mutex, wakes the poll with an ephemeral write,
and observes E_AUTH from its detached reader. All 11 ephemeral HTTP tests pass.

The device guide test asserts the actual shared contract: `unknown: true` and
no complete local answer. SQLite refuses before acquisition; the memory device
can return an incomplete empty speculative result. Both remain unknown and hold
no typing rows. The replacement recipe now passes on both stores.

Renewal provenance is deliberately conservative: arguments, viewer, literals,
and structural field/arithmetic expressions are stable; opaque builtins and
locals assigned in loops are not certified. Locals assigned under a clock- or
row-dependent branch are also not certified, even when each branch assigns an
argument. This can under-classify a safe renewal, but never grants coalescing to
a key with an unproved dependency. A regression test covers the clock branch;
all 14 language tests and the frozen durable-byte fixture pass.

The RFC's in-memory `--fresh` reader fallback is retained. Disk-backed polls
finish ephemeral-only wakes without the serving engine mutex, including bearer
rechecks. In-memory stores have no independent connection, so their final bearer
liveness check retains the existing engine fallback too. This is a narrow
exception to the blanket no-engine-on-unchanged-sequence wording in §3.3, chosen
to preserve revocation rather than cache authority across a held poll. Production
disk stores have the lock property; both modes preserve authentication.

a bearer. The old detached reader correctly fenced application generations, but
its session recheck incorrectly reused that catalog fence and returned
E_GENERATION. Session authority is independent of application tables. Its new

current wake state's store identity; it cannot expose an unfenced row transaction.
It does not prune sessions or take a writer lock. Ordinary row transaction
generation fences are unchanged. A mismatched store identity fails closed.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate round 8: copies known before the walk

Astra's review of round 7 (READY WITH CHANGES) found two Lows, both on the safe
side. A copy made inside a branch (`if assignee != null: selected = assignee;
if selected != null: return …`) was not yet known when the outer branch's exit
was judged, so what followed was charged to every call. That had been so since
round 5. The copies are now read from the whole program before the walk. The
IR names every binding once (`$selected1`), so a name is one binding, and a copy
counts only if it is never reassigned. A test pins the two placements as
equivalent. The refusal tests also now cover literal comparisons that hold
(`1 = 1`, `1 != 0`) and one that does not (`1 != 1`), which a constant answer
for every literal comparison survived before. Two guards proved to be dead
code and were dropped: one for a name bound twice, which the IR never
produces, and one for a copy of a reassigned local, which reads through to a
non-argument either way.

### 2026-09-26 — LLP 3000.017 fix round 2: capability installation and savepoints

Astra N1/N2/N3 and Opus N1 are fixed within the delta-review scope. Initial
online backend installation advances the query epoch, discards mounted answers
and expiry timers, and reruns watches before seeding generation. Both an already
published durable answer and a late in-flight answer are covered. Discovery is
complete only after a successful installation. Failed requests and schema facts
older than the poll's generation retry before another long poll can hold them
up. The local choice where the RFC is silent is 25/50/100/200/400 ms exponential
backoff capped at 500 ms, continuing while the client has credentials and mounted
watches; close aborts the wait. Stale facts never replace operation interests.
The scratch candidate's initial reset was retained, with seeding ordered after
the reset; its retry-on-next-poll alone was insufficient for bounded recovery.
Tx::rollback_to clears the lazy sequence-table existence cache after successful
rollback, so rolled-back DDL can be allocated again in the same transaction.

Added ephemeral-capability.test.mjs and the sequence_by savepoint regression.
With production sources still at 1c5dc4fd0, all four new client cases failed
(0 pass / 4 fail): Astra's real-server differential kept 1 through three
generation-2 polls while a direct read returned 2, one injected schema 503 never
recovered, a stale-schema mock failed to catch up, and a held old query was not
retired. The savepoint regression failed with `no such table: _sequences`
(0 passed / 1 failed). After the fixes, the affected client suite passes 32/32

### 2026-09-26 — LLP 3000.017 fix round 3: schema retry boundaries

N4/N5 are fixed in the online client. An observed generation change now
retires mounted snapshots and their expiry timers before awaiting schema.
Schema loading also retires outstanding query publications and withdraws
freshness. The RFC does not prescribe discovery-failure delivery: the local
choice is to re-query mounted watches every 500 ms while schema loading
suspends `/changes`. Those answers carry `fresh: false`; they deliver durable
updates even if every schema request fails or one stays held. This keeps the
existing stale-generation fence: no new poll starts with obsolete operation
interests. Successful installation restores ordinary notification-driven
refreshes. The fallback stops on close, last-watch removal, credential refusal
or terminal store refusal. Schema retries retain 25/50/100/200/400 ms backoff
and the 500 ms cap.

Schema `E_AUTH` now uses `obsoleteRefusal`, like query/poll refusals. A current
bearer refusal ends credentials with no further schema attempt; an obsolete
bearer refusal waits for an in-flight rotation and retries with its successor.
Schema dispatch also waits for rotation. Close can release the schema wait
even if a supplied fetch ignores its abort signal.

The three real-server Astra reproductions are now repository regressions in
ephemeral-capability.test.mjs, strengthened to require delivery of the durable
insert, immediate generation invalidation, and withdrawn freshness. A fourth
regression holds rotation across an obsolete schema refusal. All four fail
against a44b11b51 (0 pass / 4 fail); the original client build reproduced the
three real-server failures, and transpiling only that commit's client.ts into
the current package reproduced all four. No existing expectation changed.
The first corrected capability run passes 7/7; the expanded affected run and
complete qualification are recorded below. Evidence: target/eph-fix3-evidence/.

Only client.ts, its capability regression file, and this journal change.
There is no RFC semantic deviation, schema/type/wire-format change or budget

### 2026-09-26 — CCP L3 query withholding investigation

LLP 3000.008.002.000 lane L3 takes the brief's report-only disposition: no
diagnostic or product change. Ordinary horizon scans on a different order return
partial data; they do not alone withhold the answer. Streaming scalar totals,
extrema, speculative point/rule reads, and Following-specific coverage can
withhold the whole composition. Runtime input coverage and evaluated branches
matter. Calibration's inbox withholds while inboxLocal completes, but the
unchanged jobs-card inbox has the same horizon scalar decoration and also
withholds. A useful scalar-consumer predicate would truthfully name both,
conflicting with the brief's requirement that every card remain silent.

This is a scope conflict, not a claim that no static risk predicate exists.
A narrower expiring-maintained-view scalar predicate could catch calibration's
first failing sum and avoid the jobs card's direct count, but misses the same
failure in direct-count decorations. The chosen minimal outcome records that
option for the lead rather than adding source/name exceptions or changing cards.
No new N_ code, routing rule, schema, protected-result lifetime, or wasm byte was
introduced. No query warning is justified by order mismatch alone.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate precision: every test judged under the facts in force

Grok's review of round 7 left six shapes where the certificate charged work
that never runs (`issues/closed/20260926-snapback4-scale-certificate-precision.md`).
None claimed a constant that grows, but each weakened the proof a builder reads.
Patching them one by one would have added a sixth special case to a walk that
already had three kinds of `if`, a separate `leaves` pass that did not track
facts in order, and a `never_holds` for literals. So the walk changed shape.

`body()` now prices a body and returns whether every path through it leaves,
so there is no second pass to fall out of step. A condition becomes a `Test`:
known, an argument's presence, or unknown, combined by `not`, `and` and `or`.
It is judged three-valued under the facts in force. A branch whose facts
contradict them never runs. What follows runs only after a branch that stays,
under its facts. A `require` is the same rule: it leaves where its test fails
and states its facts for what follows. This one rule covers all six shapes and
the decided `else`. It judges facts in order inside a branch, `require 1 > 2`
and `require not true`, a presence refusal the facts contradict,
`not (assignee = null)`, and `and`, `or` and `not` of presence tests.

Two consequences needed care:

- **Facts for every program, variants only where they exist.** Presence facts
  were computed only when some scan was a planner variant, so a program without
  one found no dead code. Facts now always decide reachability, and only
  `when()` is gated, so such a program's certificate still names no variants.
- **Boolean bindings are flow-sensitive.** The compiler lowers `a and b` to
  `$b = a; if $b: $b = b`. A whole-program reading of `$b` would have been
  wrong for a user's own `known = a; if known: …; if known: known = b`, whose
  first test reads `a`. So a binding holds the test it was given, as far as the
  walk has reached. After an `if`, every binding either branch reassigned holds
  none, except the step the `if` itself is. At a loop's start, every binding
  the body reassigns holds none, since a later pass can carry a value back. Two
  tests pin the loop and branch cases. Each certified a scan as a cleanup
  backlog when it can grow.

Also: a dead `matching` no longer clears a live merge's lane bound, and a job
that returns before its sweep no longer lists it under the whole job. Dead code
still adds to the allowance, as before. The unused `reassigned` field is gone.

Evidence: eight new tests in `scale_variants.rs` (23 in all), and 23 mutants,
each killed, among them `<` read as `<=`, `not` keeping its facts, `and`
dropping its right side, no loop or branch invalidation, and a never-run
branch counted as staying. The scale, cost, check, expiry and fix targets pass:
`check` 71, `check_cost_source` 10, `expiry_writes` 32, `fix` 27,
`following_view` 2, `intent_issue_tracker` 4, `scale` 20, `scale_intent` 7,
`scale_variants` 23, `scale_windows_expiry` 7.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate precision round 1: each branch starts from the tests before it

Both families reviewed round 0. Astra returned NOT READY with two High soundness
regressions, and Grok READY WITH CHANGES with three Lows. Both High findings
came from boolean bindings, the one new mutable state in the walk:

- **The `then` arm's bindings leaked into the `else` arm.** Arms were walked in
  turn over one `tests` map, and the reassignments were invalidated only after
  both. So `known = true; if flag: (if known: known = false) else: (if known:
  return t first 2)` certified the `else` arm's scan as never running. The same
  happened inside a helper's expression block. Each arm now starts from a
  snapshot of the tests in force. The `and`/`or` step is read at the end of its
  own arm. After the `if`, the snapshot returns, and every binding either arm
  reassigned holds no test.
- **A loop's rebuilt test survived the loop.** At entry, a loop's reassigned
  bindings were cleared, but the body could rebuild one (`known = true; if
  known: known = assignee != null`) and carry it out, although the loop can
  run no times. They are now cleared again after the loop.

Grok's Lows are precision:

- **A constant side of `and`/`or` hid the other's facts.** `false or assignee
  != null` stated nothing. `facts()` now lets a side the facts decide as its
  operator's identity leave the other side to decide the whole. So
  `assignee != null and (assignee = null or false)` never holds.
- **A `require` inside an arm that always runs, or inside both arms, did not
  condition what followed the `if`.** `body()` now returns the facts that hold
  where it falls through, not only whether it leaves. After an `if`, what
  follows runs under the facts every staying arm keeps.
- **A dead assignment cleared a live binding.** Code that never runs now
  assigns nothing, in an arm or in a loop.

Astra's Low: nothing pinned `or` with a true operand, or `and` with a false one,
beside an unknown. Four refusals now do.

Evidence: 27 variant tests, 12 of them new. Astra's and Grok's repros are among
them, including the sibling-arm case inside a helper, an empty loop, a weaker
reassignment in an arm, dead assignments, constant sides, and refusals kept
after an arm. Grok's surviving mutation, both sides' facts for a true `or`, now
fails `a_constant_side_of_and_or_or_leaves_the_other_to_decide`.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate precision round 2: what a test states, rechecked

Both families reviewed round 1 READY WITH CHANGES. Astra found no soundness
failure across 1,200 generated queries and 28,800 interpreter calls, and full
certificates identical to the base for 149 operations. Grok also found no
soundness hole. Every remaining finding is precision, and round 2 takes all
but one:

- **A test's own facts can decide it the other way** (Astra).
  `(a != null or b != null) and (a = null and b = null)` states `a` and `b`
  absent, which makes the `or` false. `assume()` now evaluates the test again
  under the facts it adds and rejects a branch they contradict. This is a
  second three-valued evaluation, not a solver.
- **A straight-line reassignment holds the test it was given** (Grok).
  `known = false; known = assignee != null` read `known` as unknown. A
  reachable assignment now records its value's test and still marks the name
  written, so a branch or a loop that reassigns it still leaves it none after.
- **Literal arithmetic folds** (Grok). `require 1 + 1 = 3` never passes.
  `literal()` evaluates `+`, `-` and `*` of integers as the interpreter does.
  An overflow, which fails the call, stays unknown.
- **Tests** for `!=` between unequal literals in increasing order, `null != 1`,
  subtraction, and an `and` with a false side (Grok's surviving mutation, both
  sides' facts on a false `and`).

Not taken: a dead assignment still keeps a copy from being an alias. `copies()`
reads the whole program without the walk's reachability, so it over-charges
only. Making it reachability-aware means walking copies inside `body()`. That is
larger than the finding.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate precision round 3: a step reads its recorded test

Astra's review of round 2 found a High that round 2 itself introduced. Round
2 made a reachable assignment record its value's test. But the `and`/`or`
step still evaluated its assignment's value again after the arm, against a
map that already held the new test. A self-referential step (`known = true;
if known: known = not known`) was negated twice. `if not known` then
certified its scan as never running, although every call reaches it. That was
a false `constant`, also inside a helper's block, a merge lane's setup and a
`WriteTarget` condition. The step now takes the test its assignment recorded
where its arm ends, and `steps()` only recognizes the final assignment. Two
regressions pin the self-negation, one with a planner-variant scan. A passing
`2 * 3 = 6` kills the survivor that read `*` as `+`.

Grok's review of round 2 found the same High, and two more things. Unary minus
now folds (`require -1 > 0` never passes). An `or` with a true side holds
whatever the other side is, so its arm runs in both presence states. Tests
pin `true or assignee != null` and `assignee != null or true`. The first
lowers so the presence test never enters the `Test` at all. The second is
the one that kills the mutation taking the other side's facts.

## 2026-09-26 — Scale certificate precision round 4: the last precision Lows

Both families reviewed round 3 READY WITH CHANGES and found no soundness
defect. Astra ran 3,000 generated queries and 72,000 interpreter calls, and
compared full certificates with the base for 204 fixture operations and 214
guide operations: they matched, except for the intended dead-code reductions.
Round 4 takes the remaining precision Lows, each with a test, and every
mutation of the new code fails a test.

- **A loop's dead assignment keeps the binding's test.** `repeated()` clears the
  loop's reassigned bindings on entry and exit. It now restores, after the
  loop, any binding the reachable walk never reassigned. A reachable
  reassignment still leaves none, since the loop may have run.
- **`p or p` states `p`.** A true `or` of equal sides takes that side's facts.
  `not` of a presence test is now the opposite presence, so
  `p or not (p = null)` is the same case.
- **Integer division folds** with the interpreter's Euclidean `/` and `%`.
- **A copy keeps its own test** when its source is reassigned (Astra's test gap).
  An unknown side of a true `or` lends the other side nothing (Grok's surviving
  mutation).

One mutation survives by design. Folding `1 / 0` to `0` instead of unknown
changes no sound certificate, because a division by zero fails the call either
way. Declined, as in round 2: a dead assignment still keeps a copy from being an
alias (`copies()` reads the whole program).

## 2026-09-26 — 0.4.4 lane LT: the server knows its own p95

Implemented LLP 3000.019 §3.7 on `sb4-intent/lt-latency`, from `cfa35e161`.
The HTTP host records query, mutation and action paths, sync, change polls,
and asset upload/download in fixed histogram pairs, with counts, refusals,
nearest-rank p50/p95/p99 and exact maxima. Each operation's statistics use
7,720 bytes, plus its name/map entry. The 480 integer logarithmic buckets
cover zero through every u64 nanosecond value, including 10 µs to 10 minutes,
with at most 5% relative percentile error; no samples or row data are retained.
Invalid operation names share three fixed entries. Successful adoption keeps
surviving entries and drops retired names, bounding the registry by the active
program and seven fixed entries.

Acceptance is timestamped in the vendored HTTP parser after headers and before
body prebuffering. Total ends at response write/flush; a streamed asset's later
one-view bookkeeping is excluded. Wait ends at the first engine acquisition,
including authentication; a request that never acquires it has zero wait.
Later acquisitions remain in total. One separate mutex records the sample;
recording never acquires the engine. Refusals include top-level denials, failed
write/action envelopes, HTTP errors and failed/aborted transports, but not
nested user data or incomplete reads. These are HTTP request timings, including
held polls and action pending responses, not asynchronous handler durations.
Reset excludes requests accepted before the new window, even if they finish
later. Timings use monotonic time and a real Unix-millisecond `since`, independent
of the development clock.

Added `/dev/latency` and dev-only `/dev/latency/reset`. Dev inspection does not
take the engine; production inspection uses the existing live service-token
check, which still acquires the engine for authentication. Ordinary doctor
shows the three slowest observed total p95s and the worst wait; `--latency`
shows every entry, `--json` emits the snapshot, and `--latency --reset` starts a
new window. Reset is bound to the store identity doctor inspected, so a reused
listener port cannot reset another store's metrics. Doctor uses HTTP/1.0 for
its bounded close-only reader: an audit found that snapshots above 32 KiB
otherwise use chunked framing. The added 300-operation regression proves both
read and reset past that threshold. The bounds card owns the command recipe;
its lead and Quarry blocks remain unchanged. No new diagnostic code.

Targeted evidence: nine histogram/HTTP regressions pass, including 200,000
random samples, all bucket boundaries, bounded unknown names, request counts
and logical refusals, held-engine attribution with independent inspection,
in-flight reset, service authorization and expiry, admission refusal, and
successful asset streams plus range refusal. Two real-process CLI tests pass;
the final HTTP-framing fix also passes all four existing adoption/doctor
regressions. Whole guide: 86/86. Both ignored measurement tests were explicitly
run and passed. One million recordings measured 81.4 ns/request. Alternating
2,000 real HTTP reads per mode measured off p50/p95 269.364/376.144 µs and on
270.185/373.280 µs: median +0.821 µs (0.30%), with no visible p95 regression on
this fixture. This shared-host measurement is not a latency guarantee.

## 2026-09-26 — Lane R round 2: ownership belongs to the database

Accepted every Astra/Grok round-1 finding. Backend commands and hosts now
flock the database inode exclusively; native device processes use compatible
shared locks and exclude backend writers. The guard retains its canonical
path and descriptor, compares fstat/stat after acquisition, retries changed
names before SQLite, and validates the retained identity on later opens.
Server workers retain the guard through their SQLite lifetimes. Address
records use no-follow/nonblocking opens, descriptor regular-file checks and
0600 permissions before truncation; symlinks, FIFOs, directories and hard
links refuse with E_STORE. Removing/replacing serve.lock cannot release
ownership. Run retries cannot follow a retargeted alias into another host's
store. The witness fixture now follows the same descriptor drop order.

Native residency uses the store's generation-checked read transaction.
Stale handles return E_GENERATION, including through the public process
client. Exact page totals, actual interrupted installation with a competing
installer, address-record replacement, live database/WAL/SHM relocation,
retargeted retries, live-server device exclusion and multiple device owners
are tested. Mutants adding one byte, returning 1 GiB, committing counters
before triggers, or opening/closing an extra database descriptor all fail.
The last exposes SQLite's POSIX-lock pitfall in DELETE mode; restored locks
also coexist correctly with SQLite in WAL mode. No mutant remains.

## 2026-09-26 — bounded asset lists get their home and read authority

Fixed calibration #22's accepted-but-unservable `[image <=10000000] <=4`
shape on `sb4/image-list-assets`, in the image-list worktree. Chose element
placement: LLP 1006's one-home contract already includes lists, and the
builder wanted that form. The server now stamps each element's upload facts,
claims its row/column home, and follows that row's read rule when serving it.
Reconciliation uses asset identities: reorder retains homes and view history,
removing an element releases it, and deleting a row releases every element.
Optional/nested lists and video lists use the same traversal; `once` remains
per image and principal. Upload admission also recognizes a backend with only
list asset columns. Existing refusal codes and transactional claims are reused.

Asset ledger work is reserved before write-target lookup, including for an
empty or unchanged cell. A scalar slot reserves four examinations, two writes,
eight steps and 16 KiB scratch; each list cap multiplies the same allowance.
System retirement outside a write attempt pays the same reservation. No runtime
ceiling is raised. Asset placement remains server-side and sqlite-gated.

reorder, removal, deletion of two elements together, and per-element once/Range
behavior. Core regressions cover authoritative facts, ownership/kind/size/home
refusals and rollback, optional/nested/video lists, and a readable editor
retaining another uploader's elements. Meter tests compare 0/1/4 elements with
four scalar slots and refuse before any claim at the declared boundary. The
four core and two initial HTTP regressions all fail against the restored base
runtime; they pass with the fix. The media card's compiled `sendPhotos` example
and its two authoring-census entries landed with the implementation.

table map and the new example's missing census entries. Reservation now checks
for a real table declaration; both existing regressions pass in isolation.
Neither assertion nor any test count/timeout was relaxed.

The same pass also found two expectations tied to the old, uncharged scalar
ledger. The feed fixture now asserts both exactly four physical application
rows and six logical writes (four plus the declared claim/release pair). The
rule-probe exhaustion fixture leaves four examinations for the scalar slot so

the same control allowance. Its unchanged heap-receipt assertion exposed

## 2026-09-26 — image-list fix round 3: release across the row before claiming

Grok's remaining placement finding was column-order dependence: moving an
upload into an earlier-sorted asset column claimed before the old column
released it. A row write now queues added ids while releasing all removed ids,
then performs the claims. Every release still carries the exact table, row and
column and uses round 2's matching-home predicate. An upload still homed on
another row is refused with E_ASSET_PLACED; a failed claim rolls back both the
row and earlier releases. The change stays in the server-only asset module,
with the existing declaration reservation and scalar accounting unchanged.
LLP 3000 §7 records the ordering.

The assets card now states the legacy boundary in one short paragraph beside
removal/reorder/deletion: stored pre-placement list ids are not backfilled, a
same-id rewrite does not claim them, readers still get E_ASSET_UNKNOWN while
the upload owner can preview, and placing fresh uploads establishes homes.
These sentences follow the existing error definition so diagnostic excerpts
retain their full definition and recovery facts.

Eight new regressions cover both move directions for list and scalar columns
on memory and disk SQLite, with disk reopen before final assertions. Each
also attempts a cross-row replacement, expects E_ASSET_PLACED, and checks that

### 2026-09-27 — Lane OW round 1: ownership survives refused filesystem mutations

Merged `origin/main` at `dde688548` by fast-forward, then addressed all four
findings in the full Grok round-0 review. `private_fs` now lstats the database
and auxiliary name before opening either `-owner` or `serve.lock`, then compares
the descriptor against both pre-open and current database metadata. A suspect
post-open descriptor is intentionally forgotten without flock, chmod, read,
write, unlock or close, preserving SQLite's process-wide POSIX locks. The
same helper protects address lookup on a busy refusal. Empty owner files and
at-most-128-byte address records are the only admitted forms: these stat-only
size checks also reject a populated database renamed to an auxiliary name
when the database path no longer exists.

Both CLI ownership and native `Store::open_shared` lock the sidecar before
creating a database. A busy probe at a moved store's old path leaves that path
absent. Database link counts are checked without opening in acquisition,
native open and `Owner::path`; `nlink != 1` refuses with `E_STORE` and the
rewrite “copy the store, do not hard-link it.” Existing owners recheck their
sidecar's named inode. Native opens recheck before returning. Backend stores
and detached readers now retain the same sidecar Arc, and ordinary store
reads, writes, activation and authority transactions validate ownership too:
checking only `Owner::path` would not stop an already-open server connection.
This is the necessary extension beyond the brief's named call sites, confined
to the requested ownership hardening. No new language forms or diagnostic
codes; normal `init`/`dev`, `run`, shared devices and published busy addresses
keep their existing spellings and meanings.

Eight new regressions cover: (1) deterministic post-open hard-link/rename
aliases retaining the descriptor and SQLite's external POSIX exclusion;
(2) command/device/native busy opens creating no missing database; (3) same-
and cross-directory hard links refusing both paths and an existing owner;
(4) database renames to either auxiliary name retaining SQLite exclusion;
(5) removed/replaced sidecars revoking old guards and live connections;
(6) two real dev processes after unlink, with old reads/writes refused and
only the new server's mutation committed; (7) real-process busy probes at a
moved store's old path; (8) live native-device revocation and replacement-owner
success. Two existing invalid-file tests now expect the earlier database
hard-link refusal, keeping their unchanged-bytes assertions. The initial
post-open test used unsafe fd probes, which the core test policy rejected;
it now uses stat-only `/dev/fd` inspection and an external Python POSIX-lock
probe, with no unsafe Rust test code.

### 2026-09-27 — Lane KG: keep the approved answer through replacement authority

Implemented the 0.4.5 lane brief on `sb4-intent/kg-kept-through-authority`
from `9473e0a34`. A kept createApp observation retains the last facade-approved
answer, stale with its original since, while a replacement awaits authority.
The raw live watch owns the held answer's deadline and reset lifetime, so a
remount can peek it without extending the 30-second window. Device/server
expiry sweeps withdraw all due held answers before callbacks can roll the clock
back. Local reobservation wakeups preserve remembered server data; a raw
replacement's earlier expiry does not expire the older approved answer.
Scope resets, source refusals, facade fences and opening/replacement authority
failures still withdraw immediately. Held server expiry also invokes the
existing fallback-memory barrier, preserving newer unexpired memory while
preventing old HTTP bodies from restoring expired data after rollback.

Added internal `read-approval.ts`; changed app-client, read-observation,
read-expiry and the online/local expiry callbacks. Updated the client manual
and LLP 3000.019 §3.3 together with the code. No edit to authorized() or the
existing raw observation linger mechanism was required. No public spelling,
engine authorization, disclosure, durability, meter, version or budget changed.

The ephemeral investigation found a product race: a server-time estimate
100 ms ahead can trigger an expiry re-read before server expiry. The client
correctly withholds that expired reply, but its first-attempt server branch
lost the watch's final wakeup. Since expiry changes neither sequence nor
ephemeral epoch, the watch stayed loading. Live queries now retry rejected
server/composed replies through the ordinary publication/authority fences,
with one request per watch and 25/50/100/... ms backoff capped at 1 s. A
valid answer resets pacing; watch removal, close and sign-out prevent a late
continuation. One-shot reads keep their existing result. LLP 3000.017 §2.4
records this engineering choice; the brief did not prescribe retry pacing.

holds an explicit early estimate and replays the last real row reply once

### 2026-09-27 — `idFrom(label)`: a fixture label names a valid id

Two builders on two releases (the 0.4.3 comparative's Grok, and calibration
#23's Astra on 0.4.4) hit `E_WRITE_ID` with fixture strings and wrote the same
workaround: a hash of the label into the `mintId()` form. `snapback4/client`
now exports `idFrom(label)`, which is that mapping. It puts the first 80 bits
of SHA-256 over `["snapback4:id:v1", label]` under a zero time, in 26
Crockford digits. A derived id sorts before every minted id, as if minted at
the epoch. With all 128 bits hashed, most ids decoded as future times, and
seeded rows would have crowded a `by .id` sync window (Grok's review). It is synchronous on every host, through a small
portable SHA-256 (`src/sha256.ts`), because Web Crypto's digest is
asynchronous and Hermes has no `node:crypto`.

- The derivation is pinned by a test, so fixtures replay across releases.
- The portable hash is checked against `node:crypto` on 212 inputs, including
  astral characters and lone surrogates.
- `E_WRITE_ID`'s message, its `why` entry, `MutateOptions.id` and the README
  (still 300 lines) point to it.

The server's write records are keyed by principal and id, and nothing reads a
write id's embedded time, so a derived id is as good as a minted one. Ids were
never capabilities, and this is a name, not a secret. The operations manual
calls it in a type-checked block, which the public-function census requires.

## 2026-09-27 — Lane TK round 1: mutual live-token proof without a wire secret

Read the round-0 handoff and full Grok READY WITH CHANGES review, then fetched
and merged origin/main at 880788cc5. Merge 143d4804f preserves both journal
sides; a line-count comparison confirms neither parent's lines were lost.
On `sb4-intent/tk-token-live`, 2316fe561 replaces the bearer-secret request
with fresh client/server nonces and the specified direction-separated
HMAC-SHA256 proofs. The request binds service, unclamped days and canonical
store path/device/inode. Both MAC checks use RustCrypto's constant-time
`verify_slice`. Server nonces expire after 10 monotonic seconds; a capped
128-entry map consumes each before verification/minting. Existing loopback
peer, private-file, writer, single-header, no-Origin, no-CORS, no-store and
uniform refusal guards remain. This private door now requires a literal
loopback Host and rejects the old secret header. Offline semantics and CLI
stdout remain unchanged.

Mutual proof alone permits an active forwarding listener to intercept a
plaintext final bearer. The final reply therefore uses ChaCha20-Poly1305
under a separately HMAC-derived transcript key, including authenticated
validation errors. A relay can forward the one intended mint or deny delivery,
but cannot read its bearer or replay another mint. This adds HMAC 0.12.1 and
ChaCha20-Poly1305 0.10.1 to the CLI/server only. LLP 3000.019 §3.4 records the
protocol and this additional protection; services and SERVER.md match it.

Test commit 1e28f5e63 adds real impostor capture and forwarding listeners,
request-field/direction/replay checks, both-round Host/Origin/CORS checks,
and actual IPv4-mapped loopback and remote peers on `[::]` dev and serve.
The impostor test redirects the address hint, reproducing BSD interception
without requiring Linux's wildcard port to permit a second bind. Temporary
roots are canonicalized in token and ownership tests for Darwin's `/var`
aliases. Five deterministic unit tests pin independent MAC vectors, nonce
expiry/capacity, concurrent one-use consumption and reply integrity. Timing
was not measured; there is no flaky timing assertion. macOS execution remains
the supervisor's qualification, not a claim from this Linux host.

## 2026-09-27 — Lane DC round 7: session-scoped bound retries

Implemented the supervisor's simplification of LLP 3000.022 §4. Each queue
keeps an in-memory counter per binding fingerprint and group key, granting at
most eight replacement ids after replay confirms a recorded E_BOUND failure.
Every E_BOUND first replays the same id: success retires the interval; a bare
denial stays uncertain. Spent groups park until the next queue session, with
no refused coverage and no onDeliveryRefused. Removed persisted counters,
spending coverage, bound wakes/caps and bound tombstone carrying from the
TypeScript queue/state and Rust device collector. Manifest-only bindings,
startup barriers, held-attempt priority, fingerprint-scoped range-refusal
tombstones and the consumer TypeScript fix remain.

Eviction before the first replay needs a separate in-memory pending-id marker:
the allowance cannot be debited before replay confirms failure. If pressure
loses that id, the group waits for the next session instead of issuing fresh
initial ids. This conservative delay may include clean coverage before all
eight replacements are spent; it creates no persisted record or refusal and
restores no evicted debt. Repeated CAS edits reuse their replacement-id
reservation; an ultimately abandoned reservation may consume allowance.
An older membership retry now subtracts reported/refused coverage before
restoring recent collections. Parking advances scheduling order and yields
the pump turn, so continuous new debt in a spent group cannot monopolize it.
The LLP's E_BOUND row is two sentences; operations documentation matches.

## 2026-09-29 — macOS failures in the 0.4.9 dry run (supervisor)

The black M5's 0.4.9 dry run ran lanes PQ and WK on macOS for the first time and failed with
`== 1 failure(s) in 5759 s` (client tests; nothing published). There were four causes, none seen on Linux.

- **Worker snapshot imports.** `checked_imports` compared paths recorded by the checker with the
  canonical project root. When a recorded path passed through a symlinked ancestor (macOS `/var` is
  `/private/var`), the import was silently left out of the worker's snapshot and the worker never
  started. The parent directory is now canonicalized; the final component is still opened without
  following, so a linked helper is still refused. With the change reverted, both `automatic snapshot`
  regressions fail on the M5; with it, both pass.
- **Ledger path.** `supervised-workers` compared the printed, canonical ledger path with a
  non-canonical tmpdir.
- **Per-row hangs.** `per-row-retry` and `per-row-liveness` waited forever. With `setTimeout` mocked,
  undici's zero-delay timers on macOS never fire, so real requests stalled. The tests now wait by
  advancing only zero-delay timers; no deadline, backoff or probe delay moves.

Verified on the M5 (macOS, Node 24.18.0) and eb1000 (Linux, Node 24.13.1): per-row-retry 15/15,
per-row-liveness 17/17, supervised-workers 5/5, snapshot regressions 2/2. 0.4.9 is re-cut from the
main that includes this fix.

## 2026-10-01 — 0.4.11 fence: additive read scopes, and no silent skip

The 0.4.11 publication dry run (black M5, attempt 1, 10:00Z) failed three
`published 0.2.33 capability fence` cases (timeline-v2, recorded-attribution,
maintained-column). A current device reply on a 0.2.33 store now carries
`scopes` (LLP 3000.023 audience dependencies, added by lane PR c3c4ed0976),
for example `{profiles: [{}]}`; the fence required byte-equal answers. Every
lane's full suite had skipped the fence because `SNAPBACK4_FENCE_PUBLISHED` was
unset, so the change first surfaced at publication.

Ruling (Charlie, 2026-10-01): test-only. Device and client ship in one package
version, so a published client never reads a current reply. Dropping an
all-wildcard `scopes` on the device would also widen scope-loss invalidation:
the client treats a missing `scopes` as uncertified (`overlapsScope`,
`mergeReadScopes`). The fence's three current-vs-published comparisons (native
open, native refused adoption, current WASM after refused adoption) now permit
exactly one difference: `scopes` present on the current answer and absent on the
published one. Every other key stays exact.

The fence now runs by default on darwin-arm64 with cache
`~/.cache/snapback4/fence-published-0.2.33` (the helper already verifies registry
integrity on every run). It skips only off darwin-arm64 or with an explicit
`SNAPBACK4_FENCE_PUBLISHED=off`.

Evidence, on the 0.4.11 cut's built tree (2879c5d021, `target/debug` and wasm):
the new file passes 4/4 with the publication cache; the original file fails the
same three cases in the same tree (control); with the variable unset the fence
downloads, verifies both pinned 0.2.33 tarballs and passes 4/4. No product code
changed.

## 2026-10-02 — NX round 5: signal status, publication rollback and recorded-process custody

Addressed the round-4 Astra and Grok findings on the slim NX branch without
merging main. The CLI shim now removes its forwarding handlers before re-raising
a child's termination signal, with a 128+signal fallback if it survives. This
exit-zero defect **predates the NX lane and ships to every CLI user**, not just
native export users. Installed-shim regressions cover SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP
on Darwin and Linux. Main's open ticket
`issues/20261002-snapback4-cli-shim-signal-exit-zero.md` is absent from this branch;
the report records its resolution for the operator to close at landing.

The export wrapper requires a matching verified publication.json, including the
proved inventory and proof hash; status zero or an allowed environment skip
cannot replace that receipt. A durable publication intent precedes exchange.
Post-check failure swaps back; publisher death before the verified commit leaves
the previous tree recoverable, protected from wrapper finally and retention.
The next publisher restores under destination and export leases, or reports an
identity/custody conflict without deleting either tree. The verified receipt is
the commit point; a later crash during old-tree reclaim may leave partial old
reclamation, with the accepted new export already verified. Namespace switches
remain atomic, not a snapshot across separate reader opens.

Linux opens a pidfd, binds the birth check to that handle, and signals through
it. Darwin verifies identity, stops, verifies the stopped identity, then kills;
it never sends another signal after a mismatch. The initial check-to-STOP gap
can stop an unrelated recycled PID; it cannot safely resume that process. An
external actor can also kill/reap or resume/exit the stopped process between the
second check and numeric KILL, permitting reuse. These residual windows are
explicit in LLP 3000.030 section 15 and the report, not an absolute Darwin
PID-reuse claim. Actual parents retain their child handles. A late audit added
a group-leader birth recheck after collecting members and before any signal.

Real wrapper/shim/Rust publisher controls use a test-only syscall interposer at
both requested termination boundaries and for post-exchange mutation. Wrapper
finally preserves the exact previous inventory; next-export rollback and
retention-pressure controls pass. Zero-status missing/mismatched receipts also
fail, including environment skips. Final affected checks: Darwin witness units
26/26 and integration 53/53; Linux units 27/27 and integration 13/13; Darwin JS
export/shim 19/19 and Linux installed-shim/publication 6/6. Earlier fixture-path,
config-timeout and parallel-lease failures remain recorded; the unresolved
parallel-lease observation has a filesystem ticket. No assertion was weakened.

## 2026-10-02 — NX round 6: reconcile orphan publication markers

Read Astra's complete round-5 review on eb1000. Kept destination-first marker
deletion and added orphan-run reconciliation under run/export leases and a
nonblocking destination lock. A matching destination intent remains pending;
an absent/newer one permits removal only of this run's recorded new private

identity refuses. Later visible exports and newer pending intents stay intact.

across repeated kills. LLP 3000.030 §15 records the contract in the same change.

pre-destination-intent creation, each with existing/initially absent destination.
After the first kill, a later verified export is published, recovery is killed
twice after private-tree removal, and normal cleanup still compresses and then
prunes the abandoned run. Committed publication evidence survives compression;
rejected private bytes do not. Independent controls verify each required lock,
matching/newer destination intents and changed private identities. Pause hooks
exist only in the test executable.

The lease-release assertion now runs in an isolated subprocess, verifies
FD_CLOEXEC and deliberately forks a held descriptor before dropping its owner.
It asserts continued exclusion, releases/reaps the child and only then asserts
reacquisition. Production spawn paths can transiently inherit a lease until

## 2026-10-03 — Fence: neutral additive answer metadata

The 0.4.12 publication dry run (attempt 4) failed the three `published 0.2.33 capability fence` cases again. This time the cause was `decorationExpiry: null`, added to query answers by lane SJ. The fence had grown one hand-written exception per new key (`scopes`, then RV's `preserved`). Lanes on Linux cannot run this darwin-arm64-only fence, so each new key surfaced only at publication.

`sameAnswer` now states the rule instead. Every key the published answer carries keeps its exact value. An extra key the published release never sent is admitted only in its neutral state: `null`, `false`, `[]` or `{}`. On a store the old release wrote, new metadata must have nothing to say; a non-neutral value is a semantic change and still fails. The `scopes` and RV `preserved` exceptions are unchanged. A unit test pins the rule.

Verified on the black M5 against the 0.4.12 cut's built binary and wasm: all 4 fence cases and both allowance tests pass.

## 2026-10-03 — DR: startup banners reach the log before serving

The fourth 0.4.12 cut's Darwin dry run failed `snapback4::replay` (two tests),
as lane X27R's run had on the Apartment mini. Each test reads the stdout
readiness URL, makes one request, and then expects every startup banner on
stderr. Lane CT (b0e606306e) starts the async diagnostics writer at background
QoS, so on a loaded Mac the user-initiated request workers answered before the
starved writer had written the banners. `diagnostics::drain` now sends a
barrier through the writer's FIFO and waits, bounded at three seconds across
queue-full retries, for both destinations to be written and flushed. `serve`
calls it once, after the last startup banner and before `serve_requests`
accepts work, for both `dev` and `serve`. A timeout continues best-effort.
Request and engine threads still never wait on output, and the writer keeps
CT's QoS. LLP 3000 §7 records the rule. Unit tests cover ordering and both
bounds, and `replay` now also asserts `serve`'s startup ordering.

Lane DR measured on the Apartment mini: the replay target passed 22/22 on each
of ten consecutive runs under CPU burners (220/220), and 22/22 on eb1000. On
main 22ebfac22a, the diagnostics unit tests pass 3/3, replay 22/22, and the
reference audit passes. DR's own fence change is superseded by main 4c70334fff.

## 2026-10-03 — QF round 7: native Node and keeper-owned cleanup

Read Round 6's Astra NOT READY review in full and implemented the operator's
replacement architecture. Merged origin/main 484c94733c, including the fixed UB
baseline at 9c048bf174, in a46e58a12f; the only conflict was this append-only
journal and both complete histories are preserved. No product, Rust, original
flaky-test assertion, guard, seed or skip changed outside that main merge.

Each file now runs as native node --test with default isolation. Its native
parent's exit status supplies the test verdict. The reporter only observes
progress and diagnostic counts; the custom run() and isolation:none path is
gone. The keeper is a small Node helper held alive by stdin. On completion,

## 2026-10-03 — NL round 1: nullable unique points require non-null proof

This supersedes the preceding NL entry's first-candidate interpretation.

replica chooses from the rows it holds. Null ties can therefore produce
different complete point answers. The operator chose compile-time refusal:

selected unique key to be provably non-null, through its static type or a
null guard. Both spellings, program/rule `exists`, `created` and keyed writes
share the check. Rule short circuits and focal shape-field guards retain
presence facts. Diagnostics offer guards, a bounded population, or row id;
literal null needs replacement. Storage uniqueness, total population equality,
required-key null misses and maintained null groups remain unchanged.

including rules. Named reads still prefer a shorter total unique key when
available and check remaining equalities; plan identity is conditional on
selecting the same index without residual predicates. Nullable population

preserved. The guide, LLP 3000.013 §2.2 and closed ticket now state this rule.
Calibration #29's sorted, non-null principal keys remain legal.

## 2026-10-04 — LU round 1: bounded delivery share during continuing arrivals

Both round-0 reviewers found that the forward-key rotator could starve old work
indefinitely while a fresh one-recipient delivery arrived before every turn.
Following now uses a durable round-robin queue: new items append behind every
pending item, and an unfinished slice atomically moves its cursor and queue
position to the tail. The existing internal Work.at field holds that position;
no schema/index migration is needed. An item pending at time t among P items
gets a slice within P successful visits to its declaration, or D×P successful
background delivery turns across D fixed declarations. P is frozen at t;
later arrivals cannot extend that obligation. After service a new obligation
uses the then-current P. Cancellation/parking ends it; growing overload and
OS/commit delays do not gain a wall-clock promise. CT pacing, aged opportunities,
admission and ceilings remain unchanged. LLP 3000 §7 states the proof and the
restart/declaration-hint scope; LLP 3000.013 and the feeds guide agree.

Eight deterministic regressions cover continuing one-row arrivals before every
turn with five backfills, cleanup and multi-slice fan-out; the D×P bound, FIFO
control, atomic failure and reopen/adopt are retained. Six fail against the
round-0 selector, including all four ongoing service bounds. Later events can
reach a follower before earlier events; the final page remains sorted and
duplicate-free. A React page regression checks that ordering with overlapping
pages. The SDK and included chat surfaces derive their lists and counts from
query snapshots, not FIFO delivery notifications. The report scopes the audit
of calibration backend source separately from its unavailable frozen UI.

Correction to the preceding entry's blanket confinement claim: taskset alone
does not keep Chromium SwiftShader workers in their inherited mask. A live
thread audit found workers on 0–9 during the first round-1 attempt; that attempt
was stopped and excluded. Round 0's browser confinement was not fully proved.
The LU launcher now freezes the mask with an inherited unprivileged seccomp
filter refusing affinity changes, and the formal run audits all descendant
threads. Both final runs use CPUs 80–89; the suite witness uses 90–91. Burners
remain in owned groups and were reaped normally. Other harnesses' corresponding
audit is tracked in the Chromium-affinity follow-up; no unrelated process was
signaled and no other machine was used.

The final guarded sweep repeats 0/20/120 burners, 1,000 historical posts and a
refollow before every update, with 30 writes per shape/load and two remote
receivers. Heavy-load slower-receiver p95 is 24,645.0→892.1 ms for repost,
2,160.9→1,485.5 ms for message, and 2,278.6→657.5 ms for reaction. Each meets

## 2026-10-05 — RF: wait for the retirement fence as bounded setup

fences before a failed deletion returns, with no two-second deadline from a
clock advance. Replaced the fixed loop with the existing 60-second setup
barrier, preserving every credential, manual-seat and replacement assertion.

and conventional workers. Production code and wasm budgets are unchanged.
The serve/adoption audit found no other matching short supervisor setup wait.

returned `E_WITNESS_PROCESS: invalid /proc process group`, the signature of the
existing open inspection issue. Three isolated controls per original/fixed
binary and the entire original CLI unit target passed; they do not erase the
suite failure or establish its precise cause. All 320 client files and both
serial model files passed. The [RF report](./reports/20261005-rf-retirement-fence-wait/REPORT.md)
records commands, contracts, audit dispositions, controls and raw evidence.

## 2026-10-08 — EM round 7: preserve newer intent across concurrent producers

Astra's round-6 review found a producer-to-producer ordering left outside the
receipt repair. An older producer validated before sleep and paused before
publication; a newer producer published its valid post-sleep pair and coalesced
successfully. The older producer then overwrote that pair and rejected its own
retry. The stopped holder rejected the remaining stale pair, leaving the request
pending with no observer. Atomic rename protected complete bytes, not ordering.
Grok marked round 6 READY; Astra marked it READY WITH CHANGES for this P2.

The busy-queue producer path now locks `maintenance-wakeup.lock` across
validation, comparison and publication. Equal or later valid intent in either
the wakeup or receipt is preserved; the candidate must itself validate under the
lock and again before rename. The original expiry/sample pair is retained.
Consumers keep the round-6 receipt protocol and never acquire this writer lock.
Only producers serialize here, and no pending or active custody lease is held
while they wait. Acquisition checks cancellation/sleep/expiry at 20 ms intervals

## 2026-10-08 — App farm round 1: `run` beside a live dev, `--no-watch` staleness, `/seed` ids

The app-farm round-1 synthesis (`~/appfarm/synthesis/round-01.md` §2.1; ~270
builds on 0.4.13/0.4.14) ranked "live dev store blocks the CLI" first among
Snapback 4 clusters: 27 builds (GPT 5, Muse 22), 41 diaries. Builders ran
`run <op> --as <persona>` or `run <job>` beside `snapback4 dev`, got
`E_STORE_BUSY`, then stopped the server or rediscovered the wire
(dependency-freshness-score-0868, castle-credentials-0334,
seed-lineage-swap-0927, weed-front-0518). LLP 3000.019 §3.4 always allowed
running "the work through that server"; `run` now does, periphery only:

- When the store's owner answers `GET /dev/status` (a responsive dev host),
  a query goes to `POST /q/<op>` and a mutation to `POST /m/<op>` with the
  `x-snapback-persona` header for the principal a local run would use
  (default alice; a declared persona or `dev:<name>`), on the host's dev clock
  and adopted schema. Stdout keeps the local shape; a forwarded mutation has no
  events/meter. Stderr says it forwarded.
- Jobs go to a new dev-only `POST /dev/jobs/<job>` (`serve_maintenance.rs`): it
  enqueues one run as the system and drives chunks through `engine_work` until
  done or parked, behind earlier queued runs; `serve` refuses with `E_AUTH`.
  `/m/<job>`'s `E_OP` now names it.
- `--now`, a non-persona principal, an action, `serve` and a stopped host are
  not forwarded; those refusals keep `E_STORE_BUSY` and append the equivalent
  copy-pasteable `curl`. The status probe has a 3 s bound, so a SIGSTOPped host
  refuses instead of hanging (check_adoption's stopped-host case).
- `--no-watch` (seed-lineage-swap-0927 and weed-front-0518 lost 3 and 15+ min
  to "E_OP unknown operation" from a pinned schema): startup prints that edits
  are not re-adopted, and an unknown operation, job or argument refusal adds
  that `snapback/` changed on disk since adoption with a restart rewrite. Cost:
  one stamp of the source tree, on those refusal paths only.
- `/seed` (9 builds, archive-names-0724 lost 5 min to a bare
  `E_FIELD: missing field id`): the handler moved to `serve_dev_doors.rs` and a
  row without a string id now refuses `E_FIELD` naming the row index and table,
  why seed needs ids (it is an upsert by id: reruns update, never duplicate),
  the 26-character Crockford form with a valid example, and `idFrom`. Minting
  was rejected: it would make a rerun seed duplicate rows silently.

Core, store, rules and `contract.ts` are untouched. Tests: run_admission's
live-dev case now asserts forwarding of a job, a mutation as `dev:bob` and a
query, plus the `--now` curl refusal; a new case covers the `--no-watch`
startup line and stale refusals (also through forwarded `run`) and the seed id
refusal; check_adoption and lifecycle cases that expected `run` to refuse now
expect forwarding (or the stopped-host refusal); unit tests pin persona
mapping, the curl form and the seed example's validity. `cargo test -p
snapback4` passes except `stalled_resolver_sigint_is_bounded_journalled_and_drained`,
which fails only under the full parallel load and passes alone (unchanged
witness code). Guide, `--help` and CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS §5 describe it.

snapshot pages built as `serve_sync.rs` builds them, `observe_store`, `apply`
through `call_text`, catch-up stream. Nothing is written into a device store
directly.

The device's published answers are compared on the whole outcome record:
`complete` with `unknown` false, and known refusals. The only exceptions are
the device's `seq` (always 0) and the server-only delivery manifest. Other reads
are counted by reason, and in this generator every one is `online-only-*`.
Writes go through `admit`. A device refusal must equal the server's. A
predicted row must equal the committed one, less its `pending` marker. After
`settle` and a sync round, the device must answer as the server does.

The device has no ceiling input. Low ceilings reach it only through `call`'s
`spent` ledger, which this run used. No shipped crate changed.

100,000 cases in 875 s with 8 workers on a loaded M-series Mac (load 90–120):

- 58,499 reads compared per store with zero disagreements; at the default
  ceilings all seven meter fields agree.
- 757,317 low-ceiling positions per store: 16,920 SQLite-device disagreements
  and 29,632 memory-device disagreements, all heap or step accounting.
- 2,282 writes compared per store, with 56 disagreeing; 2,967 convergences, all
  passing.

The heap findings are the device half of the 2026-10-08 heap ruling. The device
interpreter reads a non-uniform-rule table through a per-candidate ~18 KB
decoder reservation, so both stores show it. The memory store prices scans
without SQLite's page scratch. In both, the final charge agrees and the peak
does not. Their nine signatures route to the open heap ticket.

The write finding is new: a device predicts an insert whose caller-supplied id
belongs to a row outside its partition, and the server refuses it `E_RULE`
(`issues/20261008-snapback4-device-predicts-insert-over-an-unheld-id.md`).

Three planted device faults were each caught, then reverted with the shipped
crates verified clean:

- memory scan ties reversed: 32 read disagreements;
- a complete page's last row dropped: 120 per store;
- predicted writes refused: 25 per store.

The memory store is exercised natively, with the core's `sqlite` feature on,
not as the wasm artifact. The nightly runner adds `run-devices` to its
calibration and campaign.

## 2026-10-08 — Quarry in Lean, Stage 2: a small core with its security proofs

LLP 3000.035 §5.2's model is in `snapback4/lean/`. It is a Lake project
pinned to Lean 4.34.1, with no Mathlib. `./check.sh` builds it in about 15 s
cold and under 1 s warm. The script refuses any `sorry`, `admit`,
`native_decide` or `axiom`, and audits 38 headline theorems for standard
axioms only. It also runs 30 hand-written examples taken from the guide
cards. All 30 agree.

The model was written from the language card, the guide cards, the `why`
pages and the LLPs. The interpreter, binder, `value.rs`, `key.rs` and the
device crate were not read. Each point the documents leave open is in
`lean/OPEN.md` with the model's choice: 30 points, 3 of them confirmed by a
document or corpus case. The engine has not been consulted on any of them.
The points most likely to disagree with it are these:

- R1: a probe inside a rule sees rows its own table's read rule hides.
- R2: an unnamed `update <- R` judges both old and next.
- V2: null sorts before every other kind.
- C2: a page that fills exactly has `next: null` when no candidate follows.
- W1–W4: precedence among refusal codes.
- W2: an insert of a row its writer cannot read returns null.

**What is proved**, over the executable big-step semantics:

- The scalar order is a total order. Keys are ordered lexicographically, and
  the order agrees with an order-preserving, self-delimiting key encoding.
- Scan order is determined by key order: permuting the stored rows changes
  no page.
- A query's whole outcome is a function of the viewer's visible rows. This
  covers data, `complete`, `next`, refusal and unavailability. Every
  returned row and every cursor passes its read rule. `count` is exactly the
  number of visible matches. `exists` is true exactly when a visible row
  matches. A hidden insert changes no query.
- Write authority holds for each write and for whole mutations, as a chain
  of authorized steps.
- A page that reports `complete` returned exactly the first N qualifying
  visible rows. A cut page's rows, followed by its continuation's, equal the
  uncut page. That is oracle 2, now a theorem.
- `true or e` skips `e` for every `e`, and `identity(1) + identity(2) = 3`.
- Hoare rules for each statement form are sound.

Four planted model faults each made `lake build` fail:

- a cut page reported complete;
- an eager `or`;
- a dropped insert-rule check;
- a leaking view.

**Next is the emitter and harness lane.** `lean/README.md` sketches the case
format: tagged scalars and the bound program as JSON. It also gives the
field-by-field comparison rule. `next` is compared for presence and through
continuation, never by bytes. Cut positions are not compared, because the
model's only meter is an abstract count of visible candidates.
